title: Rust
text:
Introduction: Why Rust Matters
For decades, systems programming forced engineers into an uncomfortable compromise:

Control and Speed without Safety: Languages like C and C++ provide bare-metal hardware access, deterministic resource destruction, and peak performance, but leave memory safety, thread safety, and undefined behavior to developer discipline. Decades of CVE audits prove that even the most disciplined teams cannot prevent memory corruption at scale.
Safety without Bare-Metal Control: Managed languages like Java, Go, Python, and C# enforce memory safety through automatic garbage collection and runtime checks. However, garbage collection introduces non-deterministic pause times, memory footprint overhead, and indirection that make them less suitable for low-latency systems, kernel drivers, game engines, and embedded microcontrollers.

Rust breaks this compromise by achieving compile-time memory safety without a garbage collector.

The Problem Rust Solves
Software reliability and security crises predominantly stem from memory safety bugs and concurrency defects: - Spatial memory safety violations: Buffer overruns, out-of-bounds array reads and writes. - Temporal memory safety violations: Use-after-free, double free, dangling pointers. - Concurrency bugs: Data races occurring when two threads access the same memory location concurrently with at least one writer and no synchronization.
Rust guarantees that properly written safe code cannot experience any of these defects. If your code compiles, these failure modes are mathematically disproven by the compiler’s borrow checker.


How Rust Achieves This
Rust replaces runtime garbage collection and manual memory management with three core mechanisms: 1. Ownership: Every value has a single owner bound to lexical scope. When the owner goes out of scope, the memory is deterministically freed (Drop). 2. Borrowing & References: References allow inspection or mutation of data without taking ownership. Rust enforces aliasing XOR mutability at compile time: you may have either any number of immutable references (&T) or exactly one mutable reference (&mut T), but never both simultaneously. 3. Lifetimes: The compiler tracks the validity of every reference, preventing dangling pointers across function boundaries and data structures at compile time without runtime overhead.


What You Will Learn
Across 25 comprehensive parts, seven applied engineering domains, and seven end-to-end production capstones, this book covers: - Core language syntax, primitive/compound types, and zero-cost control flow. - Deep mechanical mastery of ownership, stack vs. heap allocation, move semantics, and lifetimes. - Robust data modeling with algebraic data types (struct, enum) and expressive pattern matching. - Explicit, resilient error handling with Result, Option, and the ? propagation operator. - Parametric polymorphism with generics, trait bounds, and dynamic dispatch via trait objects. - Fearless concurrency using threads, message-passing channels, and atomic primitives. - Rust Atomics and Locks: Deep mastery of hardware-level atomics, memory ordering (Relaxed, Release/Acquire, SeqCst), memory fences, spinlocks, channels, custom Arc, OS primitives (futex, os_unfair_lock, SRW locks), and custom lock implementations. - Asynchronous programming with async/await, Future, and the Tokio runtime. - Systems-level metaprogramming with declarative macros, procedural macros, and foreign function interfaces (FFI). - Command-Line Tools in Rust: 26 chapters spanning Foundations (clap), Core Skills, Networking & Async (tokio, ratatui TUI), Testing & Distribution (assert_cmd, cross-compilation), Advanced Architecture, and 4 dedicated Capstone tools (fsearch, tudo, sysmon, devkit). - Production engineering: profiling, benchmarking with Criterion, cargo packaging, WebAssembly (wasm-pack), and embedded no_std firmware.


How to Read This Book

Linear Progression: Chapters 1 through 13 form the core foundation. Read them sequentially; each chapter relies strictly on concepts verified in preceding sections.
Complete, Runnable Code: Every listing is self-contained. Copy the code into your editor, compile it with cargo check and cargo run, and observe compiler messages.
Fight and Befriend the Borrow Checker: When the compiler rejects your code, read the compiler diagnostic carefully. Rust diagnostics are world-class teaching tools explaining what invariant was violated and how to rectify it.
Capstones & Projects: Work through the integrated capstones—including the CLI Task Manager, Parallel Pipeline, Async HTTP API, and the Command-Line Capstones (fsearch, tudo, sysmon, and devkit)—to solidify real-world architecture.



The Current State of Rust
Rust is mature, battle-tested, and officially adopted across industry leaders for core infrastructure: - The Linux kernel has official support for Rust drivers and kernel modules. - Major cloud hypervisors and networking layers (AWS Firecracker, Cloudflare Workers, Android OS) are authored in Rust. - Standards organizations and government agencies (CISA, NSA) recommend transitioning memory-unsafe codebases to memory-safe languages like Rust.


What Rust Is Not
To set clear expectations, Rust is not: - An object-oriented language with class hierarchies: Rust uses composition, traits, and algebraic data types rather than inheritance. - A rapid prototyping scripting language: Rust demands explicit thinking up front about ownership, error conditions, and data lifetimes. - Magic: Zero-cost abstractions mean you don’t pay runtime costs for high-level ergonomics; however, you must understand machine layouts and memory representation.

Installing Rust with rustup
The primary and official method for installing and managing Rust toolchains across all platforms is rustup.

Installing rustup
On Linux and macOS, install rustup via your terminal:
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
Follow the default prompts. This installs: - rustc: The Rust compiler. - cargo: The package manager and build system. - rustup: The toolchain multiplexer. - rust-std: Standard library binaries for your host architecture.


Managing Toolchains
Configure your shell environment:
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
rustc --version
cargo --version
To update your toolchain to the latest stable release:
rustup update stable

title: Your First Program: Hello World
text:
Your First Program: Hello World
Let’s begin with the canonical starting point: a minimal standalone Rust source file.

Direct Compilation with rustc
Create a file named main.rs:
// main.rs
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
Compile and run directly using rustc:
rustc main.rs
./main
Output:
Hello, world!


Deconstructing the Program

fn main() { ... }: The main function is the entry point of every executable Rust program. It takes no arguments and returns unit ().
println!(...): In Rust, names ending in an exclamation mark ! invoke macros rather than standard functions. println! parses format strings at compile time to ensure type safety.

title: Understanding rustc and cargo
text:
Understanding rustc and cargo
While rustc is the underlying compiler, production Rust projects are almost exclusively managed with Cargo.

The Role of Cargo
Cargo handles four essential engineering responsibilities: 1. Dependency Resolution: Downloading, pinning, and compiling external crates from crates.io. 2. Build Orchestration: Invoking rustc with optimal optimization flags, link arguments, and target settings. 3. Test & Benchmark Execution: Discovering and executing unit tests, integration tests, and performance benchmarks. 4. Documentation Generation: Generating standard HTML documentation directly from doc-comments.


Common Cargo Commands
cargo check   # Fast syntax and type verification without binary emission
cargo build   # Compile debug build with symbols into target/debug
cargo run     # Build and execute the binary
cargo test    # Run automated test harness
cargo doc     # Build HTML documentation for current project and dependencies

cargo new desk_service --bin
cd desk_service

Standard Directory Layout
desk_service/
├── Cargo.lock       # Exact resolved dependency graph

├── src/
│   └── main.rs      # Binary root entry point

name = "desk_service"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
The edition = "2024" flag configures the language edition. Rust guarantees backwards compatibility across editions through epoch-based stability.

title: What is Ownership and Why Does It Exist?
Stack vs Heap Memory in Rust
text:
Stack vs Heap Memory in Rust
Understanding where data lives is essential for writing efficient Rust code.

The Stack

Fast, LIFO (Last In, First Out) allocation.
All data stored on the stack must have a known, fixed size at compile time.
Primitive types, fixed arrays, and function frames live on the stack.



The Heap

Dynamic memory allocated at runtime.
The operating system locates a contiguous region of memory, marks it in use, and returns a pointer.
Slower than stack allocation; requires dereferencing pointers.
Dynamically sized types like String and Vec<T> store metadata on the stack (pointer, length, capacity) pointing to heap buffers.

text: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains

title: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains
text:
Thesis
Drop is not free. A long chain of Box nodes runs destructors one by one; mem::forget skips them and returns in nanoseconds — which is also how you leak. This chapter times dropping chains of 1 k / 10 k / 100 k nodes versus forgetting the large chain.

title: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains
text:
Mental model
  drop(head) → Drop::drop → drop(child) → …  (recursive / iterative cleanup)
  mem::forget(head) → no destructors; memory leaked unless into a global allocator you never reclaim

title: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains
text:
Worked examples
Verified with rustc 1.99.1, cargo run --release.
// chain of Box<Node>; time drop vs forget
Output:
drop chain of    1000 nodes: 21.888µs
drop chain of   10000 nodes: 267.357µs
drop chain of  100000 nodes: 4.211461ms
forget chain of  100000 nodes: 487ns
Drop scales with chain length (~4 ms for 100 k nodes here). forget on the same shape was ~0.5 µs — and leaked the graph.

title: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains
text:
Trap
Using forget to “speed up shutdown”. You trade CPU for leaks and skipped safety hooks (File flush, lock poisoning cleanup, etc.).

title: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains
text:
Boring rule
Let Drop run. If shutdown profiles show destructor cost, batch into arenas or reuse pools — do not forget application state.

Chapter Key Takeaways

Ownership rules ensure single ownership per resource and deterministic cleanup.
Stack memory holds fixed-size data; heap memory holds dynamic data referenced via stack pointers.
Move semantics transfer ownership, invalidating previous bindings to prevent double-free errors.

title: Shared and Mutable References
The Borrowing Rules Demystified
text:
The Borrowing Rules Demystified
Rust’s compiler enforces two fundamental rules regarding references at compile time:

At any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references.
References must always be valid.


Why the Rules Exist
This rule (often summarized as Aliasing XOR Mutability) prevents data races. A data race occurs when: - Two or more pointers access the same memory concurrently. - At least one pointer is writing. - There is no synchronization.
By disallowing simultaneous reading and writing through multiple aliases, Rust eliminates data races before the code ever compiles.

text: if-let Guards and cfg_select!

title: if-let Guards and cfg_select!
text:
Thesis
Rust 1.95 stabilised two small features that remove a lot of everyday boilerplate:

if-let guards let a match arm bind and test in its guard: Pat if let Some(x) = f(y) && x > 0 => …. If the guard fails, matching falls through to the next arm, just like a plain if guard.
cfg_select! is a compile-time match over cfg predicates. The first arm whose predicate is true is expanded, and _ is the fallback. It does the job the cfg-if crate has done for years, with no dependency.

Both have one sharp edge. The compiler doesn’t count guards towards exhaustiveness, and a cfg_select! where no arm is true is a hard error.

title: if-let Guards and cfg_select!
text:
Mental model



A match with if-let guards tries arm 1 (pattern matches, guard false, fall through), then arm 2 (guard true, body runs with both bindings); an unguarded arm is still needed for exhaustiveness. cfg_select! expands the first true cfg arm at compile time


An if-let guard runs after the arm’s pattern has matched. It can use the pattern’s bindings, introduce new ones, and chain more conditions with && (the same let-chain grammar that was stabilised for if in Rust 1.88). The new bindings are in scope only in that arm’s body. If any part of the chain fails, those bindings are dropped and the next arm is tried.

title: if-let Guards and cfg_select!
if-let Guards and cfg_select!
if-let Guards and cfg_select!
text:
Migrating from cfg-if
The cfg-if crate’s if #[cfg(unix)] { … } else if #[cfg(windows)] { … } else { … } maps one to one onto cfg_select! { unix => { … } windows => { … } _ => { … } }. Before you drop the dependency, check two things:

MSRV. cfg_select! needs Rust 1.95. If you publish a library with a lower rust-version, keep cfg-if until you raise it.
Expression position. cfg-if only expands to items. cfg_select! also works as an expression, so let x = cfg_select! { … }; replaces the common #[cfg] + #[cfg(not)] pair of let statements.

HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
text:
HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
After reading this chapter, you will understand why Rust’s standard HashMap uses a keyed, randomly seeded hash (currently SipHash-1-3) by default, how hash-flooding (HashDoS) attacks exploit deterministic hash collisions to degrade table operations to \(O(n^2)\), how Rust’s SwissTable architecture behaves under attack, and when it is safe to swap in non-cryptographic hashers like foldhash or FxHash.

title: HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
text:
Thesis
A hash table promises \(O(1)\) average-time lookups and insertions by mapping keys to buckets using a hash function. If an attacker can force many keys into the same bucket or probing sequence, insertion cost degrades to \(O(n)\) per operation—turning an \(O(n)\) workload into an \(O(n^2)\) CPU-exhaustion denial of service.
To prevent this vulnerability—known as a HashDoS attack—Rust’s standard library parameterizes HashMap<K, V, S = RandomState> with a keyed, randomly seeded hasher (SipHash-1-3) by default. The keys come from the operating system’s secure random source at runtime, so someone outside the process can’t work out which keys will collide.
That protection isn’t free: SipHash is slower than simple non-keyed hashes. When you generate the keys yourself (compiler symbols, internal integer IDs) and profiling shows hashing matters, a faster hasher can be worth it. The hasher is part of the map’s type, so this is a deliberate choice you make per map, after asking where its keys come from.

title: HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
text:
How a Hash Table Degrades
Standard hash tables map high-cardinality keys to finite table slots using two steps: 1. Hash the key into a 64-bit integer using a Hasher. 2. Map the 64-bit hash to a specific table index and control tag.
Rust’s std::collections::HashMap is a port of Google’s SwissTable design (via the hashbrown crate). SwissTable divides the 64-bit hash into two components: - \(h_1\) (lower bits): Used to determine the starting group index in the control byte array. - \(h_2\) (top 7 bits): stored as a one-byte tag in the control bytes, which are scanned a group at a time (16 bytes with SSE2, smaller groups on some platforms).
A lookup compares \(h_2\) with a whole group of control bytes at once. Each tag match is checked against the real key. If the key isn’t in that group and the group has no empty slot, the search moves to the next group in a fixed probe sequence. An insert follows the same path until it finds the key or a free slot.

The Attack Mechanics
In a normal distribution, hash values spread uniformly across buckets, resulting in short probe sequences and \(O(1)\) amortized insertions.
If an attacker knows the exact hashing algorithm and its seed (or if the algorithm is unseeded), they can precalculate a sequence of keys \(K = \{k_1, k_2, \dots, k_n\}\) such that every key produces identical low bits (\(h_1\)) and identical top bits (\(h_2\)).
When inserting \(n\) colliding keys into an empty SwissTable: 1. The 1st key goes straight into the first slot of its probe sequence. 2. The 2nd key has the same tag as the 1st, so the table compares the two keys, finds they differ, and takes the next slot. 3. The \(i\)-th key walks past all \(i-1\) earlier keys, with a tag match and a key comparison for each, before it finds a free slot.
(This is a simplified count, ignoring resizes and group-at-a-time scanning, but the shape is right.)
Total insertion steps for \(n\) keys: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n + 1)}{2} \in O(n^2)\]
At \(n = 20{,}000\) that is about 200 million key comparisons, for work that should take well under a millisecond. And the attacker only had to send the keys.

title: HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
section: Why a Keyed Random Hash Stops HashDoS
text:
Why a Keyed Random Hash Stops HashDoS
The root cause of HashDoS is predictability. If an attacker cannot predict the hash output for a given key, they cannot precalculate colliding key sets.
SipHash (introduced by Jean-Philippe Aumasson and Daniel J. Bernstein in 2012) is a family of pseudorandom functions designed specifically for short inputs like hash table keys. It mixes the input with a 128-bit secret key through rounds of add, rotate and xor (ARX) operations. Without the key you can’t predict the output.
std::hash::RandomState (also re-exported as std::collections::hash_map::RandomState) seeds SipHash with keys from a secure random source on the host, taken without blocking. The std docs describe this as “a reasonable best-effort”. Keys are generated once per thread and changed slightly for every new RandomState.
Because the key is secret and generated at runtime: - An attacker sending JSON payloads or HTTP headers cannot determine which string keys will collide in the server’s memory. - Two RandomStates, and so two maps made with HashMap::new(), hash the same key differently, even in one process. - Iteration order changes from run to run, and can differ between maps holding the same keys.

Historical Context
The HashDoS attack vector was popularized at the 28C3 conference in December 2011 by Alexander Klink and Julian Wälde (“Efficient Denial of Service Attacks on Web Application Platforms”). They showed hash flooding working against web platforms in many languages.
Afterwards: - Aumasson and Bernstein introduced SipHash in 2012, a fast keyed function meant for exactly this job. - Python switched str and bytes hashing to SipHash in Python 3.4 (PEP 456). - Rust’s HashMap uses SipHash-1-3 today. The std docs say the algorithm “is subject to change at any point in the future”.
A keyed hash stops the classic attack, where the attacker computes colliding keys offline. It does not make a table immune to every complexity attack. In October 2026 Orson Peters described a “black-box” HashDoS that never learns the hash function. It works on string keys that share a long common prefix: it times lookups to tell when a key comparison happened, uses that to map which buckets are occupied, and then builds keys that form one long probe chain. He demonstrated it against Rust’s standard-library table. It needs a lot of interactive access: lookup, insert and clear on the same table, with no other users disturbing it, and O(n log n) preparation steps. His suggested mitigation is to compare a full 64-bit hash before comparing keys. He also says it is unclear how far the access requirements protect you. So keep the default hasher for untrusted keys, and also cap how many entries one client can put into a table.

title: HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
text:
Program Execution Results
Build and run it:
cargo build --release
./target/release/hashdos
same key, two RandomStates: a521e11b44355f6d vs bc8555747fa86f7e
iteration order this run: ["cherry", "date", "banana", "apple"]
n=  5000  identity/benign  123.46µs  identity/evil    11.13ms  siphash/evil  175.54µs  foldhash/evil   94.72µs
n= 10000  identity/benign  228.74µs  identity/evil    49.00ms  siphash/evil  397.28µs  foldhash/evil  201.11µs
n= 20000  identity/benign  454.52µs  identity/evil   185.61ms  siphash/evil  830.29µs  foldhash/evil  433.46µs
Running it again gave different first two lines:
same key, two RandomStates: 982862aac45c489c vs b6ac8abef2f118c8
iteration order this run: ["cherry", "banana", "apple", "date"]

Analyzing the Output Pattern
When reviewing execution output across problem sizes (\(n = 5{,}000\), \(10{,}000\), \(20{,}000\)):
The times are from one release build on one machine. Treat them as indicative; the growth pattern matters more than the exact figures.

identity/benign: the keys \(0, 1, 2, \dots\) have different low bits, so the identity hash spreads them out. Time grows linearly and stays under a millisecond. A weak hash can look fine on friendly data.
identity/evil: As input size \(n\) doubles from 5,000 to 10,000 and then to 20,000, the time goes from 11.13 ms to 49.00 ms to 185.61 ms, roughly 4x for each doubling. This 4x scaling is the classic signature of quadratic \(O(n^2)\) complexity.
siphash/evil: For the same keys, the keyed hash scatters them, so time grows linearly (175 µs to 830 µs).
foldhash/evil: foldhash::fast::RandomState is seeded too, so this naive attack fails against it as well, and it is the fastest column here. That doesn’t make it SipHash’s equal against an attacker who adapts.
Randomness across runs: comparing the two runs shows two things:

a.hash_one(42) and b.hash_one(42) produce completely different hex values within the same execution.
The key iteration order of m changes between independent runs of the program.

title: HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
text:
Choosing a Hasher
You choose the hasher through the third type parameter. FastMap::default() works because the S type implements Default; otherwise use HashMap::with_hasher(s):
use std::collections::HashMap;
use foldhash::fast::RandomState as FoldRandomState;

// A HashMap type using foldhash instead of RandomState
type FastMap<K, V> = HashMap<K, V, FoldRandomState>;

let map: FastMap<String, usize> = FastMap::default();









Hasher
Algorithm Type
Seeded?
Intended Use Case




std::hash::RandomState
SipHash-1-3 today (may change)
Yes, random keys per thread, varied per instance
The default. Anything keyed by outside input: HTTP headers, JSON object keys, query parameters, user files. Designed to resist HashDoS.


foldhash (foldhash::fast::RandomState)
Fast non-cryptographic hash
Yes, per process
The default hasher of the hashbrown crate (0.17.1). The crate calls itself “minimally DoS-resistant”: enough for naive attacks like the one above, not a claim of SipHash-level resistance.


FxHash (rustc-hash crate)
Fast non-cryptographic hash used inside rustc
No, deterministic
Keys you generate yourself, such as interned IDs in a compiler pass. Never attacker-controlled keys.




Decision Rules

Untrusted Input Rule: If keys originate from HTTP headers, URL queries, JSON body payloads, or external files, or anything else influenced by the outside world, keep the default RandomState.
Trusted Pass Rule: If keys are internal integer IDs, compiler symbols, or generated in a closed loop, and profiling shows hashing is a real cost, foldhash or FxHash is a reasonable swap. For small integer keys, consider a Vec indexed by ID, which needs no hashing at all.

text:
Exercises

Measure Collision Depths: Change the evil keys to i << 16, then i << 4. Before you run each one, work out from the table size (a power of two above \(n\)) whether the low bits the table uses still all match, and predict the timings.
Build a Custom BuildHasher: Write a custom type implementing BuildHasher that accepts a manual 64-bit seed at construction, and use it to demonstrate deterministic hashing within a single run.
Profile Hasher Overhead: Create a benchmark using criterion comparing lookup times for \(1{,}000{,}000\) random string keys between SipHash-1-3, foldhash, and FxHash.

title: HashMap Hashers and Hash Flooding: Why the Default Is SipHash
text:
Key Takeaways

Rust’s HashMap defaults to SipHash-1-3 parameterized by RandomState to defend against HashDoS CPU exhaustion attacks.
Untrusted inputs forcing \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) collisions in SwissTable degrade \(O(1)\) operations to \(O(n)\), causing overall insertion workloads to balloon to quadratic \(O(n^2)\) time.
The random keys mean an outsider can’t predict which keys collide, and they also make iteration order change between runs.
foldhash and FxHash can be faster for keys you control. FxHash must never see attacker-chosen keys, and foldhash only claims minimal DoS resistance.
HashMap iteration order is non-deterministic by design; use BTreeMap or IndexMap when deterministic key ordering is required.

title: bbtree: a concurrent ordered map (and unsync BTreeMap drop-in)
text:
bbtree: a concurrent ordered map (and unsync BTreeMap drop-in)
After reading this chapter, you will understand how the bbtree 0.2.0 crate provides high-performance ordered map data structures in Rust, when to prefer BBTreeMap over standard synchronization primitives like RwLock<BTreeMap>, how to use unsync::BBTreeMap as a fast single-threaded alternative to standard BTreeMap, and how bbtree handles lock-free atomic readers alongside concurrent mutations.

title: bbtree: a concurrent ordered map (and unsync BTreeMap drop-in)
text:
Thesis
Rust’s standard library provides std::collections::BTreeMap for sorted, range-queryable key-value storage. However, std::collections::BTreeMap requires exclusive mutable access (&mut self) for insertions and updates. Sharing a standard sorted map across threads typically requires wrapping it in a synchronization wrapper like Arc<RwLock<BTreeMap<K, V>>> or Arc<Mutex<BTreeMap<K, V>>>. Under high read or write concurrency, global locks introduce severe thread contention, context switching overhead, and coarse lock granularity.
Alternatively, lock-free concurrent maps like crossbeam-skiplist offer lock-free ordered access, but skip-lists often incur higher pointer-chasing overhead and cash-miss penalties compared to contiguous B-tree node layouts.
The bbtree 0.2.0 crate resolves this tradeoff by implementing an optimized B-tree layout tailored for modern hardware. It offers two distinct map types:

bbtree::BBTreeMap<K, V>: A lock-free concurrent ordered map that allows shared reference (&self) concurrent reads and inserts without external mutexes or read-write locks.
bbtree::unsync::BBTreeMap<K, V>: A single-threaded, BTreeMap-shaped ordered map designed as a drop-in replacement for std::collections::BTreeMap with lower cache overhead and improved cache locality.

Upstream benchmark claims position bbtree as a significantly faster B-tree implementation compared to std::collections::BTreeMap and crossbeam-skiplist. While application performance varies depending on workload characteristics, bbtree provides an efficient option for concurrent lookups and single-threaded sorted storage.

title: bbtree: a concurrent ordered map (and unsync BTreeMap drop-in)
text:
Architecture and Concurrency Model
Understanding how bbtree provides concurrent access requires examining the differences between standard B-tree operations and lock-free node traversal.

Standard BTreeMap vs Concurrent BBTreeMap
In std::collections::BTreeMap, node rebalancing, key insertion, and node splitting modify internal pointers and node arrays directly. If a read occurs concurrently with a split, the reader could observe invalid references, dangling pointers, or broken invariants.
bbtree::BBTreeMap bypasses global coarse-grained locks by leveraging optimistic concurrency, fine-grained lock synchronization during structural modifications (such as node splits), and lock-free atomic reads. Readers traversing bbtree::BBTreeMap observe consistent node state without acquiring exclusive read locks.









Feature
std::collections::BTreeMap
crossbeam_skiplist::SkipMap
bbtree::BBTreeMap




Concurrency Support
Single-threaded (&mut self required)
Multi-threaded lock-free
Multi-threaded concurrent (&self mutations)


Node Structure
Contiguous B-tree arrays
Linked list nodes with levels
Contiguous B-tree nodes


Cache Locality
High
Low (pointer chasing across nodes)
High (cache-friendly contiguous memory)


Single-threaded API
std::collections::BTreeMap
N/A
bbtree::unsync::BBTreeMap


Read Synchronization
Exclusively borrowed or via RwLock
Lock-free epoch-based
Lock-free / atomic reading





API Differences and Copy Semantics
Because bbtree::BBTreeMap permits concurrent modifications via shared references (&self), reading values directly via references (such as returning &V) poses memory safety challenges: a concurrent write or update could invalidate the memory location underlying &V.
To safeguard concurrent operations without sacrificing performance, bbtree::BBTreeMap provides specialised retrieval APIs for types that implement Copy or Clone:

get_copied(&key): Copies the value associated with key if K: Borrow<Q> and V: Copy.
read(&key, f): Executes a closure f(&K, &V) -> R under temporary internal access controls, enabling atomic reads of complex or non-Copy values without returning borrowed references across thread boundaries.
get_many_copied([&k1, &k2, ...]): Batch retrieves multiple keys yielding an array of Option<V>.

In contrast, bbtree::unsync::BBTreeMap is intended for single-threaded usage where &mut self and exclusive borrowing guarantees remain standard. Consequently, unsync::BBTreeMap exposes standard borrowed retrieval methods like get(&key) returning Option<&V> and iterator accessors such as keys().

text:
When to Keep std::collections::BTreeMap
While bbtree offers competitive performance advantages for both concurrent and single-threaded workloads, standard std::collections::BTreeMap remains the standard choice in many scenarios:

Standard Library Compatibility: When interfacing with external crates or APIs requiring standard library types without external crate dependencies.
Small Memory Footprint / Small Collections: For small maps containing only a few elements, the low constant factors of std::collections::BTreeMap make it ideal.
Full Iterator and Mutation APIs: std::collections::BTreeMap provides extensive entry APIs (entry()), mutable iteration (iter_mut()), and splitting/merging APIs (split_off(), append()) that are not present in concurrent tree structures.

text: The Never Type ! and Infallible

title: The Never Type ! and Infallible
text:
Thesis
Rust has always had a type for “this expression does not produce a value”: !, the never type. panic!(), loop {} without break, return, continue, and std::process::exit all have type !, and a function declared -> ! promises never to return. Until now you could only write ! in that return position. Everywhere else — Result<T, !>, type Error = !;, impl Trait for ! — it was an unstable feature, and the standard library used a stand-in, the empty enum std::convert::Infallible.
Rust 1.100 (scheduled for 2026-11-12) stabilizes ! as an ordinary type after a decade behind a feature gate, and makes Infallible a plain alias for it. The language change is small; the error-handling consequence is real: “this operation cannot fail” now has one canonical spelling, Result<T, !>, that the compiler understands well enough to let you skip the impossible Err arm entirely.
The same release changes never type fallback to ! on every edition, which is a small breaking change for code that quietly relied on the old fallback to (). This chapter shows both sides, compiled with the current beta and stable toolchains.

title: The Never Type ! and Infallible
text:
Mental model
            ┌──────────────────── every type ────────────────────┐
            │   u32   String   ()   Vec<T>   Result<T, E>   …   │
            └───────────────────────────▲─────────────────────────┘
                                        │  coerces to any type
                                        │  (unreachable code needs no value)
                                       `!`   — no values at all

Result<T, !>   =  Ok(T) | Err(<impossible>)      → only Ok can exist
size_of::<Result<u32, !>>() == size_of::<u32>()  → no discriminant needed
Infallible     =  !   (type alias since 1.100)
Three facts carry the whole chapter:







Fact
Consequence




! has no values
Code that “holds” one is unreachable; the compiler can delete branches that need it


! coerces to any type
A diverging arm (die(…), panic!, return) fits in a match whose other arms are u32


An enum variant containing ! is uninhabited
let Ok(v) = r; is irrefutable when r: Result<T, !>; the Err arm need not be written



Infallible was the library’s way to get the same effect (an enum with no variants). Since it is now literally !, existing APIs such as TryFrom implementations whose error is Infallible work unchanged and read the same way.

title: The Never Type ! and Infallible
text:
The trap
Relying on inference to pick () for you. Code like f()?;, run(|| panic!()), or if c { Default::default() } else { return } compiled for years because the never type quietly became () when nothing else constrained it. Under 1.100 (any edition) or edition 2024 that guess is !, and the code either fails to compile — the good case, shown above — or, in the rare unsafe case the never_type_fallback_flowing_into_unsafe lint exists for, picks a different type than the author assumed. The compiler’s 1.99 lint (dependency_on_unit_never_type_fallback) points at every affected function: fix those before you bump the toolchain, not after.
The second, quieter trap is using ! as a placeholder in a public trait impl or function signature because “it can’t fail today”. ! is a promise. Replacing it with a real error type later breaks every caller who wrote let Ok(v) = …;.

title: The Never Type ! and Infallible
text:
The boring rule
Use -> ! for functions that truly never return and Result<T, !> (or Infallible until your MSRV is 1.100) only where failure is impossible by construction. Never lean on fallback: when the compiler cannot see a type, write it — f::<()>()?, || -> () { … }, () = expr;. Turn on the rust_2024_compatibility lints on older editions and clear them before upgrading.

text: Generic Const Arguments (GCA)

title: Generic Const Arguments (GCA)
text:
Thesis
On stable Rust, a const generic parameter may appear in a const argument alone ([u8; N]) or as a fully concrete expression ([u8; 1 + 1]). The moment you write [u8; N + 1] or [u8; T::ASSOC], the compiler stops you. The old escape hatch, #![feature(generic_const_exprs)] (GCE), taught everyone the shape of the problem but never became a stabilization candidate.
Generic Const Arguments (GCA) is the Const Generics project group’s replacement family of nightly features. Expressions that involve generic parameters go through an explicit gca!(…) marker (for now), each capability has its own gate (gca_adts, gca_min_const_items, gca_const_items, …), and definitional equality — not GCE’s evaluation model — decides when two const arguments match. Nothing here is stable. This chapter shows what compiles on today’s nightly, marks every feature gate, and records where the Oct 2026 blog post already drifted from the compiler.
Version note: verified on rustc 1.101.0-nightly (a30aa9064 2026-10-08). The Inside Rust post Generic Const Args and You (2026-10-02) is the design overview; on this nightly the feature formerly named generic_const_args has been renamed to gca_const_items (removed name errors say “removed in 1.100.0”), and the gca! macro lives at std::gca / core::gca. No RFC yet; the project group says polish first.
Stable const generics basics (structs/functions parameterized by const N: usize) live in Generic Functions and Data Structures. This chapter does not re-teach that.

Stable today

                 └── generic param alone

GCA (current nightly)    — mark exprs with gca!(…); equality by definition
       │
       ├── gca_adts              arrays / tuples / structs / enums in gca!(…)
       ├── gca_min_const_items   const items whose RHS is gca!(…)
       ├── gca_const_items       + opaque const items, assoc bindings, dyn, needs -Znext-solver often
       └── gca_macroless_*       experimental: insert gca!(…) for you (rough)







Fact
Consequence

Plain { N + 1 } as a const argument still cannot


gca!(…) accepts fewer expression kinds than a normal const block
gca!(N + 1) and gca!(foo()) are not automatically legal; prefer const items / ADTs that the gates support


gca_const_items requires gca_min_const_items
Enable both; incomplete-feature warnings are expected


Feature generic_const_args is gone on 1.101 nightly
Use gca_const_items (compiler points the rename)


Nothing is stabilization-ready
APIs that expose gca!(…) in public signatures are a SemVer hazard while the syntax is explicit

title: Generic Const Arguments (GCA)
Generic Const Arguments (GCA)
text:
The trap

Copy-pasting #![feature(generic_const_args)] from older posts. Removed in 1.100; rename to gca_const_items and enable gca_min_const_items with it.
Assuming gca!(…) is a full const evaluator. It is a marker for a restricted expression grammar that may mention generics. Unsupported ops fail loudly.
Stabilizing public APIs on gca!. The macroless work exists precisely because explicit gca! is considered ergonomically temporary — and also SemVer-visible.
Mixing GCE and GCA in one crate “just to make it compile”. Two incomplete models; pick GCA for new experiments.
Forgetting #![expect(incomplete_features)] / #[allow(incomplete_features)]. Without it, every build is a warning storm (or worse, depending on lint config).

title: Generic Const Arguments (GCA)
text:
The boring rule
Stay on stable const generics (N alone, or concrete exprs) for production. When you truly need generic const computation, use current nightly GCA with explicit gca!(…), gate every file with the specific features you touch, pin the nightly date in the chapter/PR, and re-run the listings after each toolchain bump — the rename from generic_const_args to gca_const_items already proved the surface moves.

text:
The boring rule

Use AsRef<T> for generic parameters that just need to read a &T (paths, bytes, strings). Implement Borrow<T> only when T’s Hash, Eq and Ord agree exactly with Self’s, and get there by delegating Self’s impls to the borrowed form. Implement Deref only for smart-pointer-like types, never to inherit methods. Test map lookups with keys in more than one form.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
Thesis
A lot of APIs have an order to them: connect, then log in, then query. Most libraries check that order at runtime, with a state field and an Err(NotConnected) when it’s wrong. Rust can check it at compile time instead. Make the state a type parameter, give each state its own impl block, and have every transition take self by value and return the next state. Calling a method in the wrong state is then a type error. Reusing an old state is a use-after-move error.
The part that makes this work is std::marker::PhantomData<S>. It is a zero-sized field that “uses” the type parameter without storing anything. This chapter builds a small type-state connection, shows the compiler errors it produces, measures what it costs at runtime (nothing), and covers the one decision you have to get right: which PhantomData.



Type-state transitions for Conn, the compile errors they produce, their size, and the marker choice


All listings were compiled with rustc 1.99.1, edition 2024.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
section: Why you need PhantomData at all
text:
Why you need PhantomData at all
Rust rejects a type parameter that no field mentions:
struct Conn<S> { host: String }
error[E0392]: type parameter `S` is never used
 --> bad3.rs:1:13
  |
1 | struct Conn<S> { host: String }
  |             ^ unused type parameter
  |
  = help: consider removing `S`, referring to it in a field, or using a marker such as `PhantomData`
  = help: if you intended `S` to be a const parameter, use `const S: /* Type */` instead

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0392`.
The error is deliberate. The compiler needs to know how Conn<S> relates to S for variance, drop checking and auto traits (Send/Sync). PhantomData<T> answers that question by saying “act as if this struct holds a T” (std docs), while taking zero bytes.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
What the compiler catches
Querying before login:
let c = Conn::new("db.internal").connect();
c.query("SELECT 1"); // not logged in yet
error[E0599]: no method named `query` found for struct `Conn<Connected>` in the current scope
  --> bad1.rs:67:7
   |
 9 | pub struct Conn<S> {
   | ------------------ method `query` not found for this struct
...
67 |     c.query("SELECT 1"); // not logged in yet
   |       ^^^^^ method not found in `Conn<Connected>`
   |
   = note: the method was found for `Conn<Authed>`

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0599`.
The note the method was found for Conn<Authed> points straight at the missing transition.
Reusing a state after it has been consumed:
let c = Conn::new("db.internal");
let a = c.connect();
let b = c.connect(); // reuse the Idle value
error[E0382]: use of moved value: `c`
  --> bad2.rs:68:13
   |
66 |     let c = Conn::new("db.internal");
   |         - move occurs because `c` has type `Conn<Idle>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
67 |     let a = c.connect();
   |               --------- `c` moved due to this method call
68 |     let b = c.connect(); // reuse the Idle value
   |             ^ value used here after move
   |
note: `Conn::<Idle>::connect` takes ownership of the receiver `self`, which moves `c`
  --> bad2.rs:19:24
   |
19 |     pub fn connect(mut self) -> Conn<Connected> {
   |                        ^^^^

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0382`.
A runtime state machine would catch neither mistake until the code ran, if at all.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
Choosing the right PhantomData
PhantomData<S> says “I own an S”, so Conn<S> takes on S’s auto traits. That matters if a state marker happens to be !Send, even though no S value ever exists:
use std::marker::PhantomData;
use std::rc::Rc;

// A state marker that happens to be !Send (it is never constructed).
#[allow(dead_code)]
struct Local(Rc<()>);

struct Owns<S>(PhantomData<S>);          // "acts like it owns an S"
struct Tag<S>(PhantomData<fn() -> S>);   // "only names S": Send + Sync, covariant

fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}

fn main() {
    assert_send::<Tag<Local>>();
    assert_send::<Owns<Local>>();
}
error[E0277]: `Rc<()>` cannot be sent between threads safely
  --> auto.rs:15:19
   |
15 |     assert_send::<Owns<Local>>();
   |                   ^^^^^^^^^^^ `Rc<()>` cannot be sent between threads safely
   |
   = help: within `Owns<Local>`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<()>`
note: required because it appears within the type `Local`
  --> auto.rs:6:8
   |
 6 | struct Local(Rc<()>);
   |        ^^^^^
note: required because it appears within the type `PhantomData<Local>`
  --> /rustc/58cf8f9c35b355199727627d07ae34a4e2846d67/library/core/src/marker.rs:811:11
note: required because it appears within the type `Owns<Local>`
  --> auto.rs:8:8
   |
 8 | struct Owns<S>(PhantomData<S>);          // "acts like it owns an S"
   |        ^^^^
note: required by a bound in `assert_send`
  --> auto.rs:11:19
   |
11 | fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}
   |                   ^^^^ required by this bound in `assert_send`

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.
Tag<Local> compiles and Owns<Local> does not. The Rustonomicon’s PhantomData table lists the options:









Marker
Variance in T
Send/Sync
T may dangle in drop glue?




PhantomData<T>
covariant
inherited from T
no (“owns T”)


PhantomData<&'a T>
covariant
Send + Sync require T: Sync
yes


PhantomData<*const T>
covariant
!Send + !Sync
yes


PhantomData<fn() -> T>
covariant
Send + Sync
yes


PhantomData<fn(T)>
contravariant
Send + Sync
yes


PhantomData<fn(T) -> T>
invariant
Send + Sync
yes



For type-state markers, where S is only a label, PhantomData<fn() -> S> is usually the most accurate choice. The struct never owns an S, so it shouldn’t inherit S’s thread-safety or drop behaviour. Use plain PhantomData<S> when the struct really does own S values in a way the compiler can’t see, such as a raw-pointer collection, because that is what keeps drop checking sound.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
When not to use type-state

The state comes from runtime data. If the server decides whether you’re authenticated, you still need Result at the boundary, as login shows. You can’t hold a Vec of connections in different states without an enum or a trait object, so mixed collections go back to runtime state.
There are many states and many shared methods. Every state you add means another impl block and more generic signatures. More than four or five states is usually a sign you want an enum.
The API is public and stable. Each state type becomes part of your public API, and renaming one is a breaking change.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
Takeaways

A type parameter plus PhantomData turns protocol order into type checking, with zero runtime cost (48 bytes in every state, measured).
Transitions consume self. A failed transition returns the old state in Err.
Out-of-order calls become E0599 and reuse becomes E0382, both at compile time.
Pick the marker on purpose: PhantomData<fn() -> S> for pure labels, PhantomData<S> only when you logically own an S.

title: The Newtype Pattern: Zero-Cost Type Safety, Validated Values and the Orphan Rule
text:
Thesis
A newtype is a tuple struct with one field: struct AccountId(u64);. It costs nothing at runtime, because it has the same size and alignment as what it wraps, but it is a different type to the compiler. That one property gives you three tools:

Values with the same representation can no longer be mixed up. Account IDs, amounts, metres and seconds all stop being “just a u64”.
A private field plus a validating constructor means that holding the type is proof the value was checked.
A local wrapper lets you implement a foreign trait for a foreign type, which the orphan rule otherwise forbids.

This chapter demonstrates each one with compiler output from rustc 1.99.1, and shows where #[repr(transparent)] becomes necessary rather than optional.



The newtype pattern: one field, a new name, zero runtime cost


All listings come from one Cargo package (edition 2024). Each one is a binary under src/bin/. The *_bug.rs files fail to compile on purpose.

title: The Newtype Pattern: Zero-Cost Type Safety, Validated Values and the Orphan Rule
The Newtype Pattern: Zero-Cost Type Safety, Validated Values and the Orphan Rule

The Newtype Pattern: Zero-Cost Type Safety, Validated Values and the Orphan Rule
text:
Pitfalls

Deref as inheritance. impl Deref<Target = String> for Email makes email.len() work, but it also adds every String method to the Email API, and email.to_uppercase() quietly returns a plain String. Implement AsRef<str> and the few methods you actually mean.
DerefMut breaks validation. It lets callers write *email = "junk".into() and skip TryFrom altogether.
pub fields remove validation the same way (section 3).
Boilerplate. Each trait you want, such as Display, FromStr, serde, or arithmetic for units, has to be derived or forwarded. #[derive] covers the standard traits, and #[serde(transparent)] serialises the newtype as its inner value. Write impls by hand where the semantics differ, as with Cents * Cents.

title: The Newtype Pattern: Zero-Cost Type Safety, Validated Values and the Orphan Rule
text:
Takeaways

A single-field tuple struct is a new type at compile time and nothing at runtime: same size and alignment, and niches are preserved.
Use newtypes for IDs and units so that swapped arguments become E0308 errors.
A private field plus TryFrom turns “was this validated?” into a type-level fact.
Add #[repr(transparent)] as soon as unsafe code or FFI relies on the layout.
A wrapper is the standard answer to E0117.

Summary

Chapter Key Takeaways

Generics monomorphize at compile time for zero runtime overhead.
Traits declare shared contracts across concrete types.
Trait bounds enforce capabilities on generic type parameters.
Trait objects (dyn Trait) provide dynamic dispatch using vtables when heterogeneous collections are needed.

title: What Lifetimes Are (and Are Not)
text:
What Lifetimes Are (and Are Not)
Every reference in Rust has a lifetime—the scope for which that reference is valid.

What Lifetimes Are Not

Lifetimes do not change how long a value lives at runtime.
Lifetimes do not allocate or free memory.
Lifetimes are purely compile-time annotations that help the borrow checker ensure references never outlive the data they point to.

title: The Lifetime Elision Rules
text:
The Lifetime Elision Rules
In common function patterns, Rust automatically infers lifetime parameters via three elision rules:

Each parameter that is a reference gets its own lifetime parameter (fn foo<'a, 'b>(x: &'a i32, y: &'b i32)).
If there is exactly one input lifetime parameter, that lifetime is assigned to all output lifetime parameters (fn foo<'a>(x: &'a i32) -> &'a i32).
If there are multiple input lifetime parameters, but one of them is &self or &mut self, the lifetime of self is assigned to all output lifetime parameters.

title: Annotating Lifetimes in Functions and Structs
Lifetime Bounds on Traits
Advanced Lifetime Patterns
text:
Advanced Lifetime Patterns

The 'static Lifetime
A reference with 'static lifetime can live for the entire duration of the program: - String literals: &'static str stored in the read-only data segment. - Owned values promoted to static duration.

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text:
Thesis
Most lifetime errors that look like “the borrow checker is being stubborn” are really about variance. Variance is the rule that decides when a type with a longer lifetime can be used where a shorter one is expected. A &'static str can be passed anywhere a &'a str is wanted, but a &mut &'static str can’t be passed where a &mut &'a str is wanted. The reason isn’t arbitrary: if it were allowed, safe code could put a dangling reference into a 'static slot.
This chapter shows the three kinds of variance in compiler output, explains why each one has to be that way, and then works through the most common real bug variance causes: the &'a mut self signature that locks a struct for the rest of its life.



Covariant, invariant and contravariant positions, with ’static outliving ’short


All listings were compiled with rustc 1.99.1, edition 2024. Every error message shown is the compiler’s actual output.

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text:
Subtyping, but only for lifetimes
Rust has no struct inheritance, so the only subtyping is between lifetimes. If 'long outlives 'short (written 'long: 'short), then &'long T is a subtype of &'short T, and a value of the first type can be used where the second is expected (Reference: Subtyping and Variance).
Variance describes how that relationship carries through a type constructor F<T>:

Covariant: if A is a subtype of B, then F<A> is a subtype of F<B>. The relationship carries through unchanged.
Invariant: F<A> and F<B> are unrelated unless A and B are the same type.
Contravariant: the relationship flips, so F<B> is a subtype of F<A>.

The variance table
From the Reference:



Type
Variance in 'a
Variance in T




&'a T
covariant
covariant


&'a mut T
covariant
invariant


*const T

covariant


*mut T

invariant


[T], [T; n], Box<T>, Vec<T>

covariant

UnsafeCell<T>, Cell<T>, RefCell<T>

dyn Trait<T> + 'a

A struct or enum is covariant in a parameter only if every field that uses that parameter is covariant in it. If fields disagree, or any field is invariant, the parameter is invariant. You can’t annotate variance yourself. To change it, you change the fields, often by adding a PhantomData marker of the right shape.

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text:
Pitfalls

Assuming Cell is “just a wrapper”. Adding a Cell<&'a T> field to a struct that used to be covariant makes it invariant. That is a breaking change for downstream code that relied on shrinking lifetimes, even though no public signature changed.
Reaching for 'static to “fix” invariance errors. Writing T: 'static or &'static everywhere makes the error go away by making the API useless for borrowed data. Find the &mut or Cell that forces invariance instead.
Reading E0499 or E0502 at face value. “Mutably borrowed in the previous iteration of the loop” on a method call usually means the method’s signature ties &mut self to a struct lifetime. Check the signature before you restructure the loop.
Unsafe code with the wrong variance. A raw-pointer container that stores *const T is covariant, but if it hands out &mut T it probably needs to be invariant. Variance mistakes in unsafe code are soundness bugs, not just inconvenient compile errors.

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text:
Takeaways

Shared references are covariant, so longer lifetimes shrink to fit.
Anything you can write through (&mut T, Cell<T>, *mut T) is invariant in T, because otherwise safe code could store a dangling reference.
Function arguments are contravariant, so callbacks that accept more are acceptable where callbacks that accept less are expected.
A struct’s variance comes from its fields, so changing a field type can be a breaking change.
&'a mut Thing<'a> locks Thing for its whole lifetime. Let the &mut self borrow have its own lifetime.

LazyLock and OnceLock
text:
LazyLock and OnceLock
Global or shared values often need one-time initialization: a compiled regex, a config snapshot, a connection pool handle. Before Rust 1.70 / 1.80 you reached for lazy_static, once_cell, or a hand-rolled Mutex<Option<T>>. Today the standard library covers the boring cases:
Prefer LazyLock for static values with a pure init function. Prefer OnceLock when initialization needs arguments, fallible setup, or happens explicitly in main / a builder. This chapter sits next to Mutex and Arc because the shared handle is often wrapped in those types later — but lazy init itself is not a lock around every read after the first.

title: LazyLock and OnceLock
text:
Mental model
first access / set()
        │
        ▼
  run init exactly once  ──►  store T
        │
        ▼
 later access  ──►  &T (no re-init)

Concurrent first accessors: one wins the init; others wait, then see the same T.
If the init closure panics, LazyLock is poisoned for the rest of the process (unrecoverable). Fail fallible work before installing into a LazyLock, or use OnceLock + Result you control.
static LazyLock<T> values are not dropped at process exit; the OS reclaims the memory. That is intentional and fine for process-lifetime data.

title: LazyLock and OnceLock
LazyLock and OnceLock
text:
Choosing among the options







Situation
Prefer




static value, infallible or expect-able init
LazyLock


Init needs CLI/env parsed in main
OnceLock + set


Fallible init with structured errors
OnceLock + Result before set


Non-Sync local cache
LazyCell / OnceCell


Mutate after init
Not these cells — use Mutex / RwLock around the data, or rebuild



LazyLock implements Deref, so *LAZY and method calls work like a plain &T after init. OnceLock exposes get, get_or_init, set, and related helpers explicitly.

title: LazyLock and OnceLock
text:
Pitfalls

Heavy work on first request path. First HTTP request paying for a huge init surprises latency SLOs — warm LazyLock during startup (let _ = &*STATIC;) if the cost matters.
Panic inside LazyLock init. Poison is permanent for that static. Prefer fallible setup with OnceLock.
Storing Mutex inside when you only needed one-time init. After init, readers of an immutable T do not need a mutex. Add synchronization only for post-init mutation.
Assuming Drop runs for static LazyLock. It does not at process exit. Flush external resources explicitly if required.
Using once_cell or lazy_static in new code on 1.80+. Prefer std unless you need an API those crates still uniquely provide.

title: MaybeUninit and Uninitialized Memory
text:
MaybeUninit and Uninitialized Memory
Safe Rust assumes every value is valid for its type: a bool is only true or false, a reference is non-null and aligned, a Vec<T> upholds its length/capacity invariants. Sometimes you need storage before those invariants hold — out-pointers, element-by-element arrays, FFI buffers. The standard tool is std::mem::MaybeUninit<T>: a wrapper that tells the compiler “these bytes might not be initialized yet.”
Do not reach for the deprecated mem::uninitialized or casual mem::zeroed on arbitrary T. Prefer MaybeUninit, initialize deliberately, then assume_init only when every validity requirement of T is met.

title: MaybeUninit and Uninitialized Memory
text:
Mental model
MaybeUninit::uninit()     ← bytes may be garbage; Drop of T does NOT run
        │
   write / ptr::write     ← initialize without dropping old (uninit) contents
        │
 assume_init / assume_init_drop
        │
        ▼
       T                  ← normal Drop and safe APIs apply







API
Role




MaybeUninit::uninit()
Allocate storage; contents uninitialized


MaybeUninit::new(v)
Already-initialized wrapper


MaybeUninit::zeroed()
Fill with 0 bytes — only valid if all-zero is a valid T


write(val)
Initialize (overwrites without dropping previous)


assume_init()
Assert fully initialized; take ownership as T


assume_init_drop()
Drop in place when you do not want ownership


as_mut_ptr() / &raw mut (*ptr).field
Field-by-field init without creating &mut to uninit fields



Dropping a MaybeUninit<T> never runs T’s destructor. If you initialized and then abandon the wrapper without assume_init / assume_init_drop, you leak resources (safe but usually undesirable).

Choosing the API



Situation
Prefer




Single value, known initializer
MaybeUninit::new or plain T


Deferred init / out-pointer
uninit + write / ptr::write


Large array filled in a loop

Struct fields in sequence
&raw mut (*ptr).field + write


Need all-zero bit pattern and it is valid
zeroed with care

title: MaybeUninit and Uninitialized Memory
text:
Pitfalls

assume_init too early — immediate UB, even for i32 / bool when bytes are still uninit.
zeroed on references / invalid enums — classic footgun; all-zero is not “safe default” for every T.
Double write without drop — leaks the first T.
Creating & / &mut to uninitialized fields — use raw pointers / &raw mut until fully init.
Transmuting &mut T to &mut MaybeUninit<T> for safe code — lets safe code invent uninit views; unsound.
Assuming Miri-silence equals production-proof — still run tests under Miri for unsafe modules when you can.

title: Custom Allocators and the Allocator API
text:
Thesis
Every Box and Vec you have written so far got its memory from one place: the global allocator. You could swap that allocator for the whole program with #[global_allocator], but you could not say “this vector lives in that arena”. The Allocator trait that would let you do so has existed since 2016, behind the nightly-only allocator_api feature, and arena crates have shipped nightly-only allocator-aware APIs for years because of it.
Rust 1.100 (scheduled for 2026-11-12) stabilizes a deliberately small slice of that design: the std::alloc::Allocator trait, the Global and System allocators as implementors, and allocator-aware constructors on exactly two containers, Box<T, A> and Vec<T, A>. Everything else (Rc::new_in, fallible try_*_in constructors, allocator-aware String and HashMap) stays unstable under a new feature name, allocator_ext.
This chapter builds two allocators on the stable surface, a counting wrapper and a bump arena. It then walks through the places where the type system and the abort-on-failure policy catch people out. Everything was compiled with the current beta, which is what becomes 1.100.

title: Custom Allocators and the Allocator API
text:
Mental model
                 Vec<T, A>  /  Box<T, A>          (A defaults to Global)
                        │  holds an A by value
                        ▼
   ┌──────────────────── unsafe trait Allocator ─────────────────────┐
   │ allocate(&self, Layout)        -> Result<NonNull<[u8]>, AllocError>
   │ deallocate(&self, NonNull<u8>, Layout)            (unsafe)
   │ grow / grow_zeroed / shrink / allocate_zeroed     (provided)
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ▲                 ▲                    ▲
        Global            System           your type, or &YourType
   (#[global_allocator]) (the OS heap)     (arena, pool, counter…)
Four facts carry the chapter:







Fact
Consequence




The allocator is a type parameter with a default: Vec<T, A = Global>
Vec<u32> and Vec<u32, System> are different types. Code written for one does not accept the other


The container stores an A
A zero-sized allocator (Global, System) costs nothing; &Arena costs one pointer; &dyn Allocator costs two


Methods take &self
Implement Allocator on &Arena (blanket impl provided) to share one arena among many containers. Interior mutability (Cell) does the bookkeeping


The trait is unsafe to implement
You promise that returned blocks are valid until deallocated, that blocks don’t overlap, and that no method unwinds. The compiler cannot check any of it



allocate returns NonNull<[u8]>, a slice pointer, so an allocator can report that it handed back more than was asked for. AllocError is a zero-sized “no” with no further detail.

title: Custom Allocators and the Allocator API
Custom Allocators and the Allocator API
Custom Allocators and the Allocator API
text:
Choosing an approach







Need
Use




Replace the heap for the whole program
#[global_allocator] with a GlobalAlloc (stable since 1.28)


Many short-lived objects freed together (parsers, per-request scratch)
A bump arena passed as &Arena to Vec::new_in / Box::new_in


Measure or limit what one subsystem allocates
A wrapper like Counting<A> around Global


Pick the allocator at run time
&dyn Allocator (two extra words per container)


Shared ownership, maps, strings in a custom allocator
Not on stable yet (allocator_ext), so keep a third-party collection for now


MSRV below 1.100
Keep using nightly-gated code or the arena crate’s own types; don’t half-adopt

title: Custom Allocators and the Allocator API
text:
The boring rule
Pass the allocator in, don’t hide it: fn f<A: Allocator>(…, alloc: A) -> Vec<T, A>. Take &[T] when you only read. Reserve capacity up front in arenas, and use try_reserve wherever running out is a normal outcome rather than a bug. Write unsafe impl Allocator only after you’ve measured a reason, and run it under Miri.

title: Arc::new_cyclic: self-referential shared ownership without a temporary Option

text:
Rules inside the closure

The closure receives &Weak<T> for the allocation under construction.
upgrade() inside the closure returns None. The strong Arc is not finished yet.
After new_cyclic returns, that same Weak upgrades normally.
Storing the Weak in the struct is the usual goal; cloning it is cheap.

title: Arc::new_cyclic: self-referential shared ownership without a temporary Option
section: Lab: self weak and parent weak

title: Arc::new_cyclic: self-referential shared ownership without a temporary Option
text:
Strong cycles versus weak parents
If both parent and child stored Arc<Node> to each other, strong_count would never reach zero and the allocation would leak for the lifetime of the process. The fix is the same as in the weak-reference material: own one direction with Arc, point back with Weak. new_cyclic does not change that rule; it only removes the bootstrap temporary when the weak handle must exist during T’s construction.

title: Arc::new_cyclic: self-referential shared ownership without a temporary Option
text:
When to use new_cyclic







Situation
Approach




Field needs Weak<Self> at birth
Arc::new_cyclic / Rc::new_cyclic


Init needs fallible work or arguments later
Build with OnceLock / builder, then Arc::new


Shared state without self-weak
Plain Arc::new


Single-threaded graph
Prefer Rc::new_cyclic (no atomics)

title: Arc::new_cyclic: self-referential shared ownership without a temporary Option
text:
Pitfalls

Calling upgrade().unwrap() inside the closure — it is always None there.
Creating a strong cycle by also storing Arc edges both ways “just in case”.
Forgetting that Weak::new() is a dangling weak (always upgrades to None), distinct from a weak produced by new_cyclic or downgrade.
Expecting Drop of T to run while weak handles still exist — weak handles do not keep T alive; after the last strong ref drops, upgrades fail and the weak slots hang until dropped.

title: Arc::new_cyclic: self-referential shared ownership without a temporary Option
Arc::new_cyclic: self-referential shared ownership without a temporary Option
text:
Design sketch: arena of nodes
For larger graphs, many codebases store nodes in a Vec or slab and use indices instead of Arc. That avoids reference-count cycles entirely. Reach for new_cyclic when shared ownership is already the API (Arc<Node> handed to tasks) and a weak self/parent handle is required at birth. Do not introduce Arc solely to call new_cyclic.

Testing upgrades
Assert upgrade().is_none() only if you are inside a controlled constructor test that still runs under the closure — usually you test after construction that me.upgrade() is Some and that dropping strong owners makes weak upgrades fail, as in the lab.

title: Arc::new_cyclic: self-referential shared ownership without a temporary Option
text:
Summary
Arc::new_cyclic installs a Weak<T> before the strong Arc<T> exists, then hands you a fully formed shared owner. Use it for self-referential shared nodes and parent weak links; keep strong edges acyclic; leave Householder-level graph ownership questions to the weak-reference chapter’s design guidance.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
After this page you can explain why iter().map(|(x, y)| x * y).sum() over f32 runs as a slow scalar loop even at -O3, speed it up with the algebraic_* float methods stabilized in Rust 1.98, and decide when to write explicit accumulator lanes instead. Both run at about the same speed, but only the lanes give the same bits on every build.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Thesis
IEEE 754 addition isn’t associative, so (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can round differently. Rust’s + on floats promises the exact IEEE result of the expression as written. That forbids the reordering a vectorizer needs, so a float reduction becomes one long dependency chain. f32::algebraic_add/algebraic_mul (and _sub, _div, _rem, likewise on f64) lift that promise per operation. The standard library docs say they “allow the compiler to optimize floating point operations using all the usual algebraic properties of real numbers,” and also that “algebraic operations are non-deterministic.” You get the speed and give up reproducibility. Writing the reassociation yourself gets you the speed and keeps reproducibility.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Mental model



Strict addition is one serial chain emitted as scalar addss; algebraic_add lets the compiler build vector partial sums but the result varies with opt level and target; explicit lanes vectorize too and give identical bits everywhere


The docs’ own example is that a.algebraic_add(b).algebraic_add(c).algebraic_add(d) may be computed as written or as (a + c) + (b + d). The rewrites allowed are deliberately unspecified. Typically they include reassociation, contraction into fused multiply-add, replacing division with reciprocal multiplication, and ignoring the sign of zero. NaN, ±Inf and -0.0 “may behave in unexpected ways.” The results are always valid floats and never undefined behavior, but unsafe code must not depend on any property of them.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Choosing between them







Need
Use




Bit-identical results across builds, targets and runs (tests with exact expectations, consensus, replay, deterministic simulation)
strict +, or explicit lanes when you need speed


Fastest reduction in a hot loop, tolerance-based checks, results that may differ between machines
algebraic_*


A specific vector width or FMA on purpose
explicit lanes, or f32::mul_add (which is exact fused multiply-add, not “maybe”)



The algebraic methods are opt-in per operation. Unlike C’s -ffast-math, they don’t change the semantics of every float operation in the crate, and they don’t add -ffinite-math-only’s assumption that NaNs and infinities never occur, the assumption that lets a compiler delete isnan checks. Only the operations you mark can be rewritten.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Things that bite

assert_eq! on an algebraic result is a flaky test. The docs say two evaluations of the same expression may differ “even within a single program run.” Compare with a tolerance, or test the strict reference.
It’s all or nothing per chain. One strict + in the middle of the fold restores the dependency chain at that point. Both the add and the multiply in the fold above are algebraic.
Iterator::sum stays strict. There’s no algebraic sum(), so write the fold (or the lanes) yourself.
const contexts work too (the methods are const since 1.98), but the docs promise nothing more about their compile-time results either.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:

Change the data generator to produce values in [-1, 1). Does the algebraic sum stay more accurate than strict, and does lanes?
Make only the multiply algebraic (acc + x.algebraic_mul(*y)). Does it still vectorize? Check the asm counts.
Change dot_lanes to 16 accumulators and compare -O3 with -O3 -C target-cpu=native. Does the result change between builds? Why not?

The new types in core::range
The permanent solution is to separate the range descriptor (the geometric interval) from the iteration cursor (the transient traversal state). This design was codified in RFC 3550 and implemented in the standard library:

Rust 1.95.0 stabilized the module core::range along with core::range::RangeInclusive and core::range::RangeInclusiveIter.
Rust 1.96.0 stabilized core::range::Range, RangeIter, RangeFrom, RangeFromIter and RangeToInclusive. (RangeToInclusive has no start, so it has no iterator type.)
The same types are re-exported as std::range, so std::range::Range and core::range::Range name one type.

These modern types represent pure bounds. When their underlying bound types implement Copy (such as usize), the range types themselves implement Copy.

text:
Summary

std::ops::Range could never implement Copy because it implements Iterator. Copying an iterator implicitly would cause silent cursor forking and confusing traversal bugs.
core::range and RangeInclusive were stabilized in Rust 1.95.0.
core::range::Range, RangeFrom, RangeToInclusive and their iterator types were stabilized in Rust 1.96.0 (and are re-exported in std::range).
Modern range types represent pure bounds and implement Copy when their bound types implement Copy.
Modern ranges do not implement Iterator. They implement IntoIterator; call .iter() or .into_iter() to create a non-copyable RangeIter cursor.
Range syntax a..b still produces legacy std::ops::Range in edition 2024. A future edition is planned to transition range syntax to modern ranges.
You can convert between legacy and modern ranges seamlessly using Range::from(a..b) and .into().
Modern ranges can directly index slices via &slice[r].
Store core::range::Range in custom types like spans and AST nodes to make them Copy, and accept impl Into<Range<usize>> in public function signatures for maximum caller convenience.

text: RwLock Is Not a Faster Mutex: Lock Choice by Measurement, and Locks Across .await

title: RwLock Is Not a Faster Mutex: Lock Choice by Measurement, and Locks Across .await
text:
Thesis
“Reads don’t conflict, so use RwLock for read-heavy data” is half right. Readers don’t logically exclude each other. But every read() still writes to the lock: it adds one to a shared reader count, and dropping the guard subtracts one. In the standard library’s Linux implementation, that is a compare-exchange and a fetch_sub on one 32-bit word. With eight threads reading, that word’s cache line moves between cores on every acquisition. When the work inside the lock is tiny, the line transfer is the cost. The readers queue for the cache line just as Mutex users queue for the lock, and adding threads makes total throughput worse.
RwLock pays off only when the read-side critical section is long enough to hide that traffic. If the data really is read-mostly and the section is tiny, the answer is to stop sharing the written word: use an atomic, or give each reader its own lock (a “big-reader” lock). This chapter measures all of these.
Async code has a second lock rule: never hold a std::sync guard across an .await. The compiler enforces it only when the future has to be Send. On a current-thread runtime the same mistake compiles and deadlocks.

title: RwLock Is Not a Faster Mutex: Lock Choice by Measurement, and Locks Across .await
text:
Mental model



RwLock readers each do a CAS and a fetch_sub on one state word, so the cache line ping-pongs; measured ns per read for tiny and 0.4 µs sections; a big-reader lock with one aligned shard per reader; the async rule about std guards across .await


What one uncontended acquisition costs, from the standard library’s futex-based implementation (library/std/src/sys/sync/rwlock/futex.rs):








Operation
Atomic work on the shared word
Notes




RwLock::read()
load, then compare_exchange_weak(state, state + 1)
falls into read_contended() (spin, then futex wait) if the CAS fails or a writer is waiting


drop of a read guard
fetch_sub(1)
wakes a writer if this was the last reader


Mutex::lock() / drop
compare_exchange(0, 1) / swap(0)
waiters sleep on a futex


AtomicU64::load
none: a plain load
the line can stay shared in every core’s cache



The std source also fixes the priority policy. is_read_lockable returns false whenever the writers-waiting bit is set, and a comment in the same function calls these “writers, which have priority over readers”. So on Linux this RwLock is writer-preferring. That matters for the trap at the end of the chapter.

title: RwLock Is Not a Faster Mutex: Lock Choice by Measurement, and Locks Across .await
RwLock Is Not a Faster Mutex: Lock Choice by Measurement, and Locks Across .await
RwLock Is Not a Faster Mutex: Lock Choice by Measurement, and Locks Across .await
text:
The boring rule

Choose a lock by measuring it. Use Mutex by default. Use RwLock only when read sections are long, hundreds of nanoseconds or more (Case 2). For read-mostly data with tiny sections, stop sharing the written word: an atomic for a scalar, or per-reader shards for larger data. Never take a second read guard on the same RwLock while you hold one. In async code, a std::sync::Mutex is fine as long as the guard lives in a block with no .await. If it must cross an .await, use tokio::sync::Mutex. Remember that the compiler catches this only where Send is required.
