text: Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work

title: Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
text:
Thesis
Tokio and Rayon are both thread pools, and both size themselves to “one thread per CPU” by default. They do opposite jobs. Tokio’s workers wait for many things at once and must come back to the scheduler quickly, at every .await. Rayon’s workers compute and are expected to stay busy until the job is done. Call par_iter() from inside an async handler and a Tokio worker stops polling futures until Rayon finishes. Do that on enough workers at the same time and the whole service freezes. Timers fire late, health checks time out, and connection pools look exhausted even though the database is idle.
The fix is not to avoid either library. Give each its own lane: async code hands CPU work to Rayon with rayon::spawn, awaits the result on a tokio::sync::oneshot channel, and limits how many batches are in flight with a Semaphore. This chapter measures the difference with a heartbeat timer, shows how the thread budget changes under a CPU limit, and covers the panic case that turns a bad request into a dead process.

title: Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
text:
Mental model
 inline (wrong)                              separate lanes (right)

 Tokio worker 1: [handler ── par_iter ──────]   Tokio worker 1: [handler] await ... [reply]
 Tokio worker 2: [handler ── par_iter ──────]   Tokio worker 2: [tick][tick][tick][tick]
 ...  every worker blocked: no polling,                 │ rayon::spawn      ▲ oneshot
      timers late, sockets unread                       ▼                   │
                                                Rayon pool:   [evaluate ─────────────]







Fact
Consequence




A Tokio worker runs one task until it returns Poll::Pending
Synchronous work between two .awaits blocks every other task queued on that worker


par_iter() called outside the Rayon pool blocks the calling thread until the work is done
Inline Rayon in a handler is blocking code, however parallel it looks


rayon::spawn queues a job and returns immediately
The handler can .await a channel and give its worker back to Tokio


Both pools default to available_parallelism() threads
Two default pools mean 2× oversubscription. available_parallelism honours CPU affinity and cgroup quotas, so it shrinks under a container CPU limit


Rayon’s queue has no limit
Without a semaphore, a traffic burst becomes an ever-growing queue of CPU work

title: Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
text:
The boring rule

Async handlers never call Rayon (or any long CPU loop) directly. They take a semaphore permit, rayon::spawn the work, and await a oneshot whose closed state is an error, not a panic. Both pools get explicit thread counts from the CPU request, Rayon has a panic handler, and small batches stay sequential.

title: Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
text:
Try this

Add a sequential threshold to handle_offloaded (if batch.len() < 200 { return evaluate_seq(&batch) }) and measure tick lag with 20-item batches. Is it acceptable to run that much work inline?
Replace rayon::spawn with tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || evaluate(&batch)). Compare tick lag and total time, and count threads with ls /proc/$(pidof lanes)/task | wc -l during the run.
Set the semaphore to 64 permits and then to 1. Record total time and tick lag for each, and explain why neither number moves much while per-request latency does.
Wrap the job body in catch_unwind and send Result<u64, String> so the handler can report which input failed.

title: Sans-IO Protocol Design: State Machines Without Sockets
text: Sans-IO Protocol Design: State Machines Without Sockets

title: Sans-IO Protocol Design: State Machines Without Sockets
text:
Thesis
A network protocol is a state machine. Sockets, timers, and async runtimes are drivers. Sans-IO (without I/O) keeps those layers apart: the protocol accepts bytes, clocks, and app intents through ordinary methods, and returns transmits and events through ordinary methods. No UdpSocket, no tokio::spawn, no Instant::now() hidden inside the library. The driver owns the socket and the clock; the protocol owns the rules.
That split buys three things operators and library authors care about. Tests run without ports or sleeps — feed a slice, advance a fake Instant, assert. The same crate works under Tokio, a blocking loop, or no_std with a custom timer. Composition becomes stacking machines (handle_input / poll_transmit) instead of colouring every call site async. This chapter builds a length-prefixed framer that way, proves it with byte-at-a-time reassembly and time travel, and names the traps that turn a clean machine into a busy-loop.

title: Sans-IO Protocol Design: State Machines Without Sockets
text:
Mental model
  application                         driver (you write)
       │                                    │
       │  send("ping")                      │  socket.send / recv
       ▼                                    │  sleep / select / epoll
  ┌─────────────────────┐                   │
  │  protocol state     │  poll_transmit ▶──┘
  │  (pure &mut self)   │◀── handle_input ── socket bytes
  │                     │◀── handle_timeout ─ Instant from driver
  │                     │  poll_event    ▶── app messages / errors
  │                     │  poll_timeout  ▶── next wake Instant
  └─────────────────────┘







Idea
Consequence




Protocol methods never block
&mut self is enough; no Mutex, no channels inside the machine


Time is an argument
Tests jump five seconds with t0 + Duration::from_secs(5)


Output is polled, not pushed onto a socket
One event loop can multiplex many protocols on one fd


Incomplete input stays in a buffer
Drivers must keep calling handle_input / handle_timeout or progress stalls



The Python community documented the pattern at sans-io.readthedocs.io. In Rust it shows up in production stacks such as Quinn’s quinn-proto, Cloudflare’s quiche, Firezone’s connlib, and the sansio::Protocol trait used by WebRTC.rs — different APIs, same inversion: policy does not call I/O; I/O drives policy.

title: Sans-IO Protocol Design: State Machines Without Sockets
Sans-IO Protocol Design: State Machines Without Sockets
text:
The trap
poll_timeout that never advances. If handle_timeout does not clear or push the deadline forward, a Tokio select! or epoll loop wakes, calls handle_timeout, sees the same deadline, and spins the CPU. Always pair “return a deadline” with “on fire, change state so the next poll_timeout is None or later”.
Calling Instant::now() inside the machine. That re-couples tests to wall time and makes “five minutes idle” take five minutes. Pass now in; take Instant only in the driver.
Doing I/O in poll_transmit. The method must return bytes (or a Transmit), not send them. The moment it touches a socket, every test needs a socket and every embedder inherits your runtime choice.

title: Sans-IO Protocol Design: State Machines Without Sockets
text:
The boring rule

Protocol crates expose handle_input / handle_timeout / poll_transmit / poll_event / poll_timeout (or an equivalent push/pull trait). They take time as a parameter, allocate no sockets, spawn no tasks, and leave the event loop to the application. Tests feed byte slices and fake Instants; production drivers bind those methods to one UDP socket or one Tokio task.

title: Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It
text: Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It

title: Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It
text:
Thesis
Async Rust has one universal cancellation protocol, and it is very easy to trigger: drop the future. A future is an inert state machine that only advances when it is polled. Once it is dropped it never runs again, and it stops at whichever .await it was parked on. You don’t need to call drop yourself. tokio::select! drops every branch that loses, tokio::time::timeout drops the future when the deadline fires, and try_join! drops the siblings of the first error. Because parents own their children, cancellation propagates down the whole call tree.
That makes two different questions worth asking about every .await:

Cancel safety is a local property of one future: if I drop it before it completes and create it again, is that a no-op? mpsc::Receiver::recv passes. read_exact and Sender::send(msg) fail.
Cancel correctness is a property of the whole system: if this future is dropped here, is any invariant, message, or cleanup lost? Dropping a cancel-unsafe future is a bug only when it breaks something you care about. Losing a half-read frame during shutdown is fine. Losing it in a select! loop is not.

This chapter reproduces the four bug shapes behind most production cancellation incidents and fixes each one. The fixes follow Rain’s “Cancelling Async Rust” (RustConf 2025) and Tokio’s own cancel-safety documentation.

title: Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It
text:
Mental model



select!, timeout and try_join! drop the losers; read_frame dropped at its second await loses the header; remedies are cancel-safe APIs, not cancelling, and whole invariants


A future can only be cancelled at an .await, because that is the only place it gives control back. So the audit question for any async fn is concrete: at each .await, what has this future already done that would be lost or left half-done if it never resumed?








Operation (Tokio 1.53)
Cancel safe?
What a drop loses




mpsc::Receiver::recv, broadcast::Receiver::recv, watch::Receiver::changed
yes
nothing


TcpListener::accept, AsyncReadExt::read / read_buf, AsyncWriteExt::write / write_buf
yes
nothing (no data was read or written)


tokio::time::sleep, StreamExt::next
yes
nothing


AsyncReadExt::read_exact, read_to_end, read_to_string
no
bytes already read into the future’s buffer


AsyncWriteExt::write_all
no
how much was written


mpsc::Sender::send(msg)
no
msg itself, which moved into the future


Mutex::lock, RwLock::read/write, Semaphore::acquire, Notify::notified, Sender::reserve
partially
your place in a fair queue


async { a.await; b.await } built from cancel-safe parts
no
whatever a produced

title: Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It
Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It
Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It
text:
The boring rule
Treat every .await as a place where your future may stop forever. Race only cancel-safe operations in select! and timeout, and do the real work in the handler body. Keep progress (buffers, messages, half-built state) outside the future that might be dropped. Use reserve + permit.send, read_buf into a persistent buffer, or a future pinned outside the loop and polled by &mut. Never hold a broken invariant across an .await. Code that must finish goes in a tokio::spawned task, because dropping a JoinHandle detaches the task and doesn’t cancel it.

title: Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It

title: async fn in Traits vs dyn Trait: Desugaring, Send Bounds and Boxing
text: async fn in Traits vs dyn Trait: Desugaring, Send Bounds and Boxing

title: async fn in Traits vs dyn Trait: Desugaring, Send Bounds and Boxing
text:
Thesis
Since Rust 1.75 you can write async fn directly inside a trait. That works well for static dispatch. It stops working at two points that every library author eventually reaches:

dyn Trait. A trait with an async fn is not dyn compatible, so Box<dyn Store> is a compile error.
Send. The future that async fn returns has a hidden type, and callers can’t add + Send to it. Generic code that spawns onto a multi-threaded runtime therefore can’t prove the future is thread-safe.

Both problems come from the same desugaring: async fn get(&self) -> u32 means fn get(&self) -> impl Future<Output = u32>. Each implementor returns its own, differently sized state machine. A vtable can’t hold “a function returning some unknown-size type”, and a bound you never wrote can’t be assumed.
This chapter reproduces all three compiler diagnostics on rustc 1.99.1 and fixes them with two moves: desugar by hand to add + Send, then add a boxed, dyn-compatible twin trait. The dynosaur and async-trait crates automate the same boxing. Everything here uses only std, including a ten-line block_on, so you can run it without Tokio.



Three shapes of an async trait: plain async fn (not dyn compatible, no Send), desugared impl Future + Send (static dispatch), boxed DynStore twin (dyn dispatch)

title: async fn in Traits vs dyn Trait: Desugaring, Send Bounds and Boxing
async fn in Traits vs dyn Trait: Desugaring, Send Bounds and Boxing
async fn in Traits vs dyn Trait: Desugaring, Send Bounds and Boxing
text:
The compiler’s own warning
Compiling the same trait as a library makes the compiler warn you before any caller hits the problem:
warning: use of `async fn` in public traits is discouraged as auto trait bounds cannot be specified
 --> lint.rs:2:5
  |
2 |     async fn get(&self, key: u32) -> u32;
  |     ^^^^^
  |
  = note: you can suppress this lint if you plan to use the trait only in your own code, or do not care about auto traits like `Send` on the `Future`
  = note: `#[warn(async_fn_in_trait)]` on by default
help: you can alternatively desugar to a normal `fn` that returns `impl Future` and add any desired bounds such as `Send`, but these cannot be relaxed without a breaking API change
  |
2 -     async fn get(&self, key: u32) -> u32;
2 +     fn get(&self, key: u32) -> impl std::future::Future<Output = u32> + Send;
  |
The async_fn_in_trait lint fires only for public traits, because the problem belongs to downstream users. The suggestion it prints is fix number one.

Choosing between them








Need
Use

The boxing cost is a heap allocation per call, not per object. In an I/O-bound service that is noise next to a syscall. In a tight loop of in-memory lookups it may not be, so measure it before building the hot path on dyn. I didn’t benchmark it here.

title: async fn in Traits vs dyn Trait: Desugaring, Send Bounds and Boxing
text:
Takeaways

async fn in a trait is sugar for -> impl Future. Both its dyn incompatibility and its missing Send follow directly from that hidden, per-impl return type.
For public traits, write the desugared form with + Send. That moves the error to the implementor that caused it.
Get dyn by boxing the future in a second trait with a blanket impl, and keep the zero-cost trait for generic code.
The + Send decision is part of your semver contract.

text:
Summary

Chapter Key Takeaways

Futures are poll-driven state machines executed by a runtime.
Tokio provides a work-stealing multithreaded async runtime.
Pin prevents memory moves of self-referential generator frames.
Async code avoids thread exhaustion on high-concurrency I/O workloads.
Dropping a future cancels it at its current .await: race only cancel-safe operations in select! and timeout, and keep progress outside futures that may be dropped.

C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text: C-Variadic Functions and VaList

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
Thesis
Since Rust 1.99 (October 2026) you can define functions with a C variable argument list — unsafe extern "C" fn f(fmt: *const c_char, args: ...) — not just call foreign ones like printf. The ... parameter arrives as a core::ffi::VaList, which is layout- and ABI-compatible with the platform’s C va_list, so you can read arguments yourself or hand the whole list to a C v* function such as vsnprintf.
That closes a long-standing FFI gap: a Rust library can now implement a C header that contains void log(int level, const char *fmt, ...), sentinel-terminated APIs in the style of execl, or plugin callback tables that expect variadic slots — without a C shim file.
The feature is deliberately sharp. A variadic list carries no count and no types. Every read is an unsafe promise that the caller sent exactly what you are about to take. The job of this chapter is to make that promise small, explicit, and checked by the C compiler wherever possible.

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
Mental model
C caller                       Rust callee (unsafe extern "C" fn f(fixed, ap: ...))
─────────                      ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
f(2, "x", 3.5f)                ap: VaList          ← va_start happens for you
   │  default argument               │
   │  promotions:                    ├─ ap.next_arg::<*const c_char>()   ← va_arg
   │   char/short → int              ├─ ap.next_arg::<c_double>()        ← va_arg
   │   float      → double           │
   ▼                                 ├─ ap.clone()                       ← va_copy
registers / stack per ABI            │
                                     └─ drop(ap)                         ← va_end







C
Rust 1.99




void f(int n, ...) (definition)
unsafe extern "C" fn f(n: c_int, mut ap: ...)


va_list ap; va_start(ap, n);
implicit — ap is the started VaList


va_arg(ap, int)
unsafe { ap.next_arg::<c_int>() }


va_copy(dst, src)
let dst = src.clone();


va_end(ap)
Drop of the VaList


void vf(int n, va_list ap)
unsafe fn vf(n: c_int, ap: VaList<'_>)



Rules the compiler enforces:

The definition must be unsafe. Callers cannot be checked, so the function is unsafe to call.
ABI must be "C" or "C-unwind" for a Rust-bodied definition (other ABIs are only allowed for declarations in extern blocks, or naked functions written in assembly).
The ... parameter needs a name in a definition (args: ...), and it must be last.
Only promotion-safe types can be read. next_arg::<T>() requires the (nightly-only) trait VaArgSafe; on stable you just use the concrete types it is implemented for: c_int/c_uint and wider integers, c_double, and raw pointers. f32, i8, u16, and bool are rejected because C never passes them through ... unpromoted.

Rules the compiler cannot enforce: how many arguments there are, and what type each one has. Those come from a protocol — a count, a format string, or a sentinel — that you document in the # Safety section and, ideally, encode in the C header.

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
The trap
Treating next_arg as if it were type-checked. It is a raw read guided only by your protocol. Every one of these is undefined behaviour, and none produces a compile error in the callee:

Reading past the end. There is no length; next_arg on an exhausted list reads whatever is in the next register or stack slot. A missing sentinel in Case 2 walks off into garbage pointers.
Reading the wrong type. Caller passes long long, you read c_int; caller passes double, you read a pointer. The VaList docs allow only compatible types: identical types, same-size integers whose value fits both, compatible pointers, or *const c_void ↔︎ *const u8/i8.
Trusting integer widths across platforms. c_long is 64-bit on Linux x86_64 and 32-bit on Windows x86_64. Read c_long when the C side passes long, not i64. The VaArgSafe docs say implementations for i32/usize “shouldn’t be relied upon directly”; spell the C type.
Re-reading a consumed list. After vsnprintf(…, ap) the list is spent; use ap.clone() before the first consumer if you need two passes.
Panicking out of an extern "C" function. A panic that reaches an extern "C" boundary aborts the process. If unwinding through C is genuinely intended, use "C-unwind"; otherwise catch and convert errors to return codes, as rlog does with its None branch.
Calling your own variadic from Rust. Rust callers get none of the C header’s format checking. Give Rust code a normal, safe function (fn log(level: Level, msg: &str)) and keep the variadic entry point for C.

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
The boring rule

A C-variadic function in Rust is a thin, unsafe, #[unsafe(no_mangle)] door for C callers. It reads arguments only under a documented protocol — a count, a format string handed to libc’s v* functions, or a NULL sentinel — reads only C-spelled promoted types (c_int, c_uint, c_long, c_double, pointers), clones before any second pass, never unwinds through extern "C", and ships with a C header carrying format(printf, …) or sentinel so the caller’s compiler checks what the callee cannot.

Checklist before merging:

# Safety section states the exact protocol (how many, which types, how the list ends).
Real formatting is delegated to vsnprintf/vfprintf; you do not reimplement % parsing.
Every read type is a core::ffi C type or a raw pointer.
The C header has __attribute__((format(printf, N, M))) or __attribute__((sentinel)), and CI builds C callers with -Werror=format.
Rust-side callers use a safe non-variadic API instead.

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
Try this

Add rlog_count(void) to rlog.rs that returns how many messages have been logged (an AtomicU32), call it from main.c, and confirm it prints 3.
Remove (char *)NULL from the rjoin_len call in main.c, rebuild with -Wall, and read the warning. Then delete __attribute__((sentinel)) from the header and observe that the warning disappears while the bug remains — that is why the attribute is part of the API.
Write vrlog(int level, const char *fmt, va_list ap) in Rust taking ap: VaList<'_>, make rlog a one-line forwarder to it, and export both. Call vrlog from a C wrapper function that does its own va_start/va_end.
Change vformat to pass ap (not ap.clone()) to the measuring vsnprintf call. Explain why the second call is now undefined behaviour even if it appears to work on your machine.
Run rustc --print native-static-libs for your target and wire the result into a Makefile rule so the link line is never guessed.

title: FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
text:
FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
Rust’s bool is not a C int. Across the extern "C" boundary it must follow the platform ABI: on x86-64 SysV, a _Bool / bool return is a byte whose bits 1–7 are zero (bits above that are undefined). If the compiler forgets to zero-extend, a C caller that reads the return as bool can observe values like 16 instead of 0 or 1—and then every if (flag) in C becomes a landmine.
Rust 1.99.0 shipped a regression that dropped that zero-extension for FFI bool returns on several x86_64 targets. 1.99.1 (2026-10-15) restored it. This chapter is the incident report you want next to the FFI chapter: what broke, how to see it in a register dump, who is affected, and what to do on a pinned toolchain.

title: FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

State the x86-64 ABI rule for returning bool / _Bool
Reproduce the 1.99.0 miscompile with a tiny Rust cdylib + C main
Recognize the missing andb $0x1, %al (or equivalent zero-extend) in disassembly
Upgrade to 1.99.1 (or pin 1.98.x / avoid bool at the boundary) as mitigation

title: FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
text:
Thesis

Safe Rust returning bool to C is only as trustworthy as codegen’s ABI lowering. A missing zero-extend is a silent miscompile: the source looks right, the bit in %al does not.

title: FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
text:
Mental model
  Rust: (flags & 1) == 1     →  i1 in LLVM
                │
                ▼
  ABI: return bool in %al with bits 1–7 cleared
                │
     1.98.0:  mov %edi,%eax ; and $1,%al ; ret   ✓
     1.99.0:  mov %edi,%eax ; ret                ✗  (raw 0x10 survives)
     1.99.1:  zero-extend restored               ✓







Layer
What went wrong in 1.99.0




LLVM IR
zeroext on i1 returns was dropped for x86_64 SysV (related fallout from broader scalar-extension changes)


Machine code
No mask/extend before ret


C caller
(int)ret can print 16 when input was 0x10



Primary tracker: rust-lang/rust#163911. Fix release notes: Announcing Rust 1.99.1.

title: FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
text:
Case 2 — Who was affected
Per the issue and write-ups circulating with 1.99.1:

Targets: x86_64 SysV-style environments (Linux, musl, FreeBSD, Android, many bare-metal x86_64 configs). aarch64 / loongarch64 reproductions in the report masked correctly.
Surface: Rust functions with extern "C" (or other C-like ABIs) that return bool, especially when compiled with optimizations so LLVM folds the compare into a raw register move.
Not required: unsafe in the callee body beyond FFI—the export itself is the hazard. Callers in C/bindgen glue are where symptoms show up (wrong branch, wrong printf, corrupted flag packing).

If you ship a cdylib / staticlib consumed by C/C++/other languages, inventory -> bool at the boundary.

title: FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
text:
Case 3 — Mitigations

Upgrade: rustup update stable → 1.99.1 or newer, then rebuild all Rust artifacts that cross FFI (don’t assume an old .so is fine).
Temporary pin: Stay on 1.98.x until you can move, if 1.99.0 is already in CI.
ABI hygiene: Return u8 (0/1) or c_int at the boundary and convert explicitly:

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn rust_fn_returning_u8(flags: u8) -> u8 {
    u8::from((flags & 0x1) == 0x1)
}

Test in CI: Keep a C (or cc crate) smoke test that passes a non-0/1 pattern in the low byte’s upper bits and asserts a clean 0/1 out—exactly the repro above.

title: FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
text:
The trap

Assuming “it compiled and linked” means ABI correctness—miscompiles return successfully.
Only testing true/false inputs that already clear high bits (0 and 1), which hide the bug.
Upgrading rustc in the developer laptop but shipping libraries built with 1.99.0 in a Docker layer.

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
Rust’s type system is supposed to make use-after-free impossible in safe code. Issue rust-lang/rust#164250 (opened 2026-10-13, labels I-unsound, P-high, A-variance, A-borrow-checker) shows a counterexample: no unsafe keyword, yet a Drop impl can observe a dangling reference. A minimized form has compiled since Rust 1.4 (2015). This chapter is the incident card next to the unsafe / FFI chapters: what breaks, how to reproduce on current stable, and what to audit in your own crates — not a claim that everyday application code is doomed.

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

State the bug in one sentence: lifetime bounds on a type are not fully enforced when a covariant field is assigned after construction
Reproduce the MyType / Drop smuggling pattern on rustc 1.99.0
Separate “malicious Drop” exploitability from accidental UAF in ordinary code (per the Types Team note on the issue)
Know where to watch for fixes (Types Team / Project Zero work; do not “patch” this in user code with unsafe)

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
Thesis

If the compiler accepts a shorter-lived reference into a field whose type promised a longer lifetime, Drop runs with a lie. Safe code can then read freed stack memory — the soundness bug is in the type checker, not in your unsafe blocks.

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
Mental model
  struct MyType<'a, 'b: 'a, 'c>(&'c mut &'a str, &'b str);
       │                              │
       │                              └─ field 1: covariant in 'b
       └─ Drop assumes 'b: 'a (and related bounds) still hold

  construction:  MyType(&mut me_out, "")     // '' is 'static-ish / long enough
  later assign:  q.1 = &local_string;        // shorter 'b sneaks in
  scope ends:    Drop runs → *me_out = dangling
  after scope:   print(me_out) → UAF







Piece
Role




Covariance on a field
Allows treating a shorter lifetime as a longer one when unifying / assigning


Lifetime bounds on the struct ('b: 'a, 'a: 'static, …)
Documented intent; not re-checked thoroughly on field assignment in this bug


Drop
Runs while the type system still believes the long lifetime


No unsafe in the repro
The unsoundness is accepting the program, not an explicit transmute



The Types Team note on the issue: this would be P-critical on novelty grounds, but an 11-year-old hole that stayed unnoticed is hard to hit by accident; exploiting it generally needs an intentionally malicious Drop. Treat production risk as real but not “rewrite everything tomorrow”.

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
The trap
Hearing “safe Rust UAF” and concluding the borrow checker is worthless, or conversely dismissing #164250 because it needs a malicious Drop. The accurate posture: the invariant failed in a narrow variance/bounds corner; the ecosystem still relies on that invariant; P-high means the Types Team treats it as urgent work.

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
The boring rule
If you implement Drop and store references (or callbacks over references), construct the value with the final references in place when you can, and treat “assign a shorter borrow into a field that was typed longer” as a compiler bug to report — not a pattern to build on. Pin a toolchain; upgrade when the fix lands on stable.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
section: The mechanism, from the ELF spec
text:
The mechanism, from the ELF spec
The System V gABI defines SHT_INIT_ARRAY as “an array of pointers to initialization functions”. Its dynamic-section chapter says those functions are executed by the dynamic linker in the order their addresses appear in the array. The .fini_array entries run in reverse order. So a constructor is nothing more than one pointer-sized value that lands in that section.
Rust gives you the two tools you need:

link_section “specifies the section of the object file that a function or static’s content will be placed into.”
used “forces a static to be kept in the output object file … even if it’s never used or referenced by any other item in the crate.”

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
text:
Real output (rustc 1.99.1, x86_64 Linux, glibc 2.41)
$ rustc --edition 2024 -O before.rs -o before && ./before
[early_init] running before main
main: INIT_CALLS = 1
main: before touching CONFIG
[LazyLock] initialising on first use
main: CONFIG = mode=fast
main: CONFIG again = mode=fast
The constructor ran once, before main’s first line. The LazyLock ran once, inside main, on first dereference, and not again on the second.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
text:
Drop #[used] and it silently disappears
Here is the same file with only the #[used] line removed:
$ rustc --edition 2024 -O nouse.rs -o nouse
warning: function `early_init` is never used
warning: static `EARLY_INIT` is never used
warning: function `libc_write` is never used
warning: 3 warnings emitted
$ ./nouse
main: INIT_CALLS = 0
main: before touching CONFIG
[LazyLock] initialising on first use
main: CONFIG = mode=fast
main: CONFIG again = mode=fast
It still compiles, it still runs, and the constructor is gone. The section headers show why:
$ readelf -S before | grep -A1 init_array
  [22] .init_array       INIT_ARRAY       0000000000050e48  0004ee48
       0000000000000018  0000000000000000 WAo       0     0     8
$ readelf -S nouse | grep -A1 init_array
  [22] .init_array       INIT_ARRAY       0000000000050db8  0004edb8
       0000000000000010  0000000000000000 WAo       0     0     8
Without #[used] the array holds 0x10 bytes (two 8-byte pointers that were already there, contributed by the C startup objects and the standard library — I did not trace which is which). With it, the array holds 0x18 bytes, so our entry is the third pointer. Nothing references EARLY_INIT, so the compiler treats it as dead and drops it. The only clue is the dead-code warning. If you treat warnings as noise, or #![allow(dead_code)] is set at crate level, nothing tells you.
Two more details from the reference: #[used] only keeps the item in the object file, and “the linker, however, is still free to remove it.” In this binary the linker kept it, because .init_array is a section the linker preserves. With a custom section name and --gc-sections, you would need to check again.
If you dump the raw bytes with readelf -x .init_array before, they are all zeros. This is a position-independent executable, so the pointers are filled in at load time by R_X86_64_RELATIVE relocations, not stored in the file. Don’t conclude the entry is missing from the hex dump; count the section size instead.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
section: Edition 2024: link_section is an unsafe attribute
text:
Edition 2024: link_section is an unsafe attribute
In the 2024 edition, export_name, link_section and no_mangle must be written as unsafe(...). These attributes control linking in a global symbol namespace, and getting them wrong can cause UB from otherwise safe code. The plain spelling is a hard error:
$ rustc --edition 2024 plain.rs
error: unsafe attribute used without unsafe
  --> plain.rs:19:3
   |
19 | #[link_section = ".init_array"]
   |   ^^^^^^^^^^^^ usage of unsafe attribute
   |
help: wrap the attribute in `unsafe(...)`
Under --edition 2021 the same file builds, and the constructor runs ([early_init] running before main). Migrating to 2024 adds the unsafe(...) marker; it doesn’t change what the attribute does.
The unsafe marker is honest. Code in .init_array runs:

before std has finished setting up its runtime (for example, the main thread’s name and the stack-overflow handlers on Unix);
in an order you only partly control, across crates and shared libraries;
with no way to catch a panic. Unwinding out of an extern "C" fn aborts the process.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
section: What to do instead, most of the time
text:
What to do instead, most of the time
std::sync::LazyLock (stable since 1.80) covers almost every “I need a global initialised once” case:

it runs on first access, inside main, with the full standard library available;
it is thread-safe;
it needs no linker, unsafe attribute, or platform-specific section name.

The output above shows the difference in timing: before touching CONFIG prints before the initialiser does.
Reach for a real constructor only when something has to happen before any user code. Examples include registering with a plugin host that dlopens your cdylib, or self-registering test cases or types across crates, which is what inventory-style crates are for. Even then, use ctor rather than the hand-rolled version. It knows each platform’s section name (its docs show .init_array on Linux, __DATA,__mod_init_func on Apple, .CRT$XCU on Windows), and in its 1.x API it makes you write #[ctor(unsafe)] to acknowledge the same caveats.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
text:
Checklist

#[used] on the static, or it is silently removed.
#[unsafe(link_section = ".init_array")] on edition 2024.
extern "C" fn() signature, with no arguments and no panics.
Body uses only libc-level calls and atomics: no println!, allocation-heavy work, or thread spawning.
Verified by section size (readelf -S), not by the zero-filled hex dump.
Asked first whether LazyLock solves it, and the answer is usually yes.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
Your crate’s minimum supported Rust version (MSRV) is not just a property of your own code. It is a property of the whole dependency graph that Cargo.lock pins. One cargo update can pull in a transitive dependency, two or three levels down, that needs a newer compiler than you promised. Your source is unchanged, and the build breaks for everyone on the older toolchain. This chapter shows that break with real crates, then fixes it with the tools Cargo has shipped since 1.84: package.rust-version, resolver "3" (the MSRV-aware resolver, default in edition 2024), cargo add’s MSRV awareness, --ignore-rust-version, and --locked.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain why a dependency with an old MSRV can still break your MSRV build
Read Cargo’s requires Rust 1.xx annotations and its “rustc … is not supported” error
Switch a project to the MSRV-aware resolver and see what it downgrades and why
Tell when the resolver cannot help (your own version requirement is too new)
Make CI check the MSRV with the committed lockfile

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
Thesis

rust-version is a promise about the build graph, not just your crate. Since Cargo 1.84 the resolver can keep that promise for you. With resolver "3" it prefers dependency versions whose own rust-version fits yours. It only does that if you opt in (edition 2024, resolver = "3", or config), if dependencies declare rust-version, and if your version requirements leave it room.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
Mental model
  Cargo.toml requirement      →   resolver picks a version    →   Cargo.lock    →   rustc checks every
  url = "2.5"                     (newest that matches;            pins it          package's rust-version
                                   resolver 3: newest that                          at build time
                                   ALSO fits your rust-version)



One package with rust-version 1.85; resolver 2 picks transitive versions needing Rust 1.86/1.88 and fails, resolver 3 picks older compatible ones and builds










Knob
Where
Effect




package.rust-version = "1.85"
Cargo.toml
Your MSRV. Cargo refuses to build on an older rustc. cargo add and resolver "3" use it to choose versions


resolver = "3"
[package] or [workspace]
Default for edition 2024. Sets incompatible-rust-versions = "fallback"


resolver.incompatible-rust-versions
.cargo/config.toml / CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_RUST_VERSIONS
allow (old behaviour) or fallback (prefer compatible, use incompatible only if nothing else matches). Respected since Cargo 1.84


--ignore-rust-version
CLI
Build or resolve as if no rust-version were set


--locked
CLI
Fail instead of changing Cargo.lock



“Your Rust version” for the resolver is the workspace’s rust-version. If that is unset, Cargo uses the toolchain you are running (Case 5).

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
Worked examples
Run on Debian 13 x86_64 with the distribution toolchain rustc 1.85.1 / cargo 1.85.1. This box has no rustup toolchain installed and none was installed for this chapter. The current stable release is Rust 1.99 (Cargo 1.99, 2026-10-01). Running an older compiler is the situation this chapter is about. One difference on a current Cargo, from the Cargo changelog: Cargo 1.92 reworded the rust-version incompatibility error, so your message text will differ. The behaviour shown here has been stable since resolver v3 was stabilised in Cargo 1.84. Crate versions are whatever crates.io served on 2026-10-17. Rerunning later may pick newer versions, but the mechanism is the same.
Run the labs in order. They share /tmp/msrv-lab. Each one is a bash script you can paste.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
section: Case 1 — The break is two levels down
text:
Case 1 — The break is two levels down
url declares rust-version = "1.63". idna declares 1.57. Neither is the problem.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-01-break.sh — a direct dep with an old MSRV, a transitive dep with a new one
set -uo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/msrv-lab && mkdir -p /tmp/msrv-lab/src && cd /tmp/msrv-lab
cat > Cargo.toml <<'TOML'
[package]
name = "msrv-lab"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"          # resolver "2": rust-version of deps is ignored
rust-version = "1.85"

[dependencies]
url = "2.5"               # url itself declares rust-version 1.63
TOML
cat > src/main.rs <<'RS'
// src/main.rs — parse one URL so the dependency is really used
fn main() {
    let u = url::Url::parse("https://docs.rs/url/latest/url/").expect("valid URL");
    println!("host = {}", u.host_str().unwrap_or("?"));
}
RS
cargo --version
cargo generate-lockfile 2>&1
cargo fetch -q              # download now so later output is only about resolution
echo '--- who pulls in the ICU crates?'
cargo tree -i icu_normalizer --edges normal 2>&1
echo '--- build on this toolchain'
cargo build -q 2>&1 | head -20
echo "[cargo build exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}]"
cargo 1.85.1 (d73d2caf9 2024-12-31)
    Updating crates.io index
     Locking 35 packages to latest compatible versions
      Adding icu_collections v2.3.0 (requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding icu_locale_core v2.3.0 (requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding icu_normalizer v2.3.0 (requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding icu_normalizer_data v2.3.0 (requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding icu_properties v2.3.0 (requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding icu_properties_data v2.3.0 (requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding icu_provider v2.3.1 (requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding idna_adapter v1.2.2 (requires Rust 1.86)
--- who pulls in the ICU crates?
icu_normalizer v2.3.0
└── idna_adapter v1.2.2
    └── idna v1.1.0
        └── url v2.5.8
            └── msrv-lab v0.1.0 (/tmp/msrv-lab)
--- build on this toolchain
error: rustc 1.85.1 is not supported by the following packages:
  icu_collections@2.3.0 requires rustc 1.88
  icu_locale_core@2.3.0 requires rustc 1.88
  icu_normalizer@2.3.0 requires rustc 1.88
  icu_normalizer_data@2.3.0 requires rustc 1.88
  icu_normalizer_data@2.3.0 requires rustc 1.88
  icu_normalizer_data@2.3.0 requires rustc 1.88
  icu_properties@2.3.0 requires rustc 1.88
  icu_properties_data@2.3.0 requires rustc 1.88

[cargo build exit 101]
Even with resolver "2" (the edition 2021 default), Cargo 1.85 annotates each pick with (requires Rust 1.88), but it still locks those versions. The build then fails before compiling anything: rustc checks every package’s rust-version against itself. cargo tree -i shows the path. icu_normalizer comes from idna_adapter, which comes from idna, which comes from url. None of those is in your Cargo.toml. This is the “one transitive update breaks the build” failure, and it can happen to a crate whose own code has not changed in years.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
section: Case 2 — Let the resolver keep the promise
text:
Case 2 — Let the resolver keep the promise
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-02-fallback.sh — same manifest, MSRV-aware resolver (resolver "3")
set -uo pipefail
cd /tmp/msrv-lab
sed -i 's/^rust-version = "1.85"/rust-version = "1.85"\nresolver = "3"             # default for edition 2024; needs Cargo 1.84+/' Cargo.toml
grep -E '^(edition|rust-version|resolver)' Cargo.toml
echo '--- re-resolve against rust-version 1.85'
cargo update 2>&1
echo '--- build and run'
cargo run -q 2>&1
echo "[cargo run exit $?]"
edition = "2021"          # resolver "2": rust-version of deps is ignored
rust-version = "1.85"
resolver = "3"             # default for edition 2024; needs Cargo 1.84+
--- re-resolve against rust-version 1.85
    Updating crates.io index
     Locking 8 packages to latest Rust 1.85 compatible versions
 Downgrading icu_collections v2.3.0 -> v2.1.1 (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88)
 Downgrading icu_locale_core v2.3.0 -> v2.1.1 (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88)
 Downgrading icu_normalizer v2.3.0 -> v2.1.1 (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88)
 Downgrading icu_normalizer_data v2.3.0 -> v2.1.1 (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88)
 Downgrading icu_properties v2.3.0 -> v2.1.2 (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88)
 Downgrading icu_properties_data v2.3.0 -> v2.1.2 (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88)
 Downgrading icu_provider v2.3.1 -> v2.1.1 (available: v2.3.1, requires Rust 1.88)
 Downgrading idna_adapter v1.2.2 -> v1.2.1 (available: v1.2.2, requires Rust 1.86)
--- build and run
host = docs.rs
[cargo run exit 0]
The same manifest and the same registry give a different lockfile. Each Downgrading … (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88) line is the resolver telling you what it held back and why. You do not have to add pins or = requirements by hand, and when you later raise rust-version, a plain cargo update brings the newer versions back. Here resolver = "3" is set explicitly while keeping edition 2021. Moving to edition = "2024" gets the same default.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
section: Case 3 — cargo add is MSRV-aware; your requirement wins over the resolver
text:
Case 3 — cargo add is MSRV-aware; your requirement wins over the resolver
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-03-direct.sh — cargo add is MSRV-aware; a hand-written requirement can still force a break
set -uo pipefail
cd /tmp/msrv-lab
echo '--- cargo add picks the newest uuid that fits rust-version'
cargo add uuid --features v4 2>&1 | grep -vE '^ +[-+] |Features:'   # drop the feature list
grep '^uuid' Cargo.toml
cargo build -q 2>&1 && echo '[build ok]'

echo '--- now ask for a version that only exists for newer Rust'
sed -i 's/^uuid = .*/uuid = { version = "1.28", features = ["v4"] }/' Cargo.toml
cargo update -p uuid 2>&1
cargo build -q 2>&1 | head -4
echo "[cargo build exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}]"

[cargo build exit 101]
cargo add chose 1.26.1 and said why (ignoring uuid@1.28.0 (which requires rustc 1.89.0)). Once the manifest says "1.28", no version that satisfies the requirement fits Rust 1.85. The resolver’s fallback policy is documented to pick an incompatible version instead of failing resolution, so cargo update succeeded, and cargo build refused. The fix is in Cargo.toml: lower the requirement or raise rust-version. The resolver cannot fix it.

cd /tmp/msrv-lab
sed -i 's/^uuid = .*/uuid = { version = "1.26", features = ["v4"] }/' Cargo.toml
cargo update -q -p uuid --precise 1.26.1 2>&1
sed -i 's/^rust-version = "1.85"/rust-version = "1.90"/' Cargo.toml
echo '--- claim a newer MSRV than this toolchain'
cargo build -q 2>&1 | head -4
echo "[cargo build exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}]"
echo '--- the escape hatch (use when you know why)'
cargo build -q --ignore-rust-version 2>&1 && echo '[build ok with --ignore-rust-version]'
sed -i 's/^rust-version = "1.90"/rust-version = "1.85"/' Cargo.toml

echo '--- CI: the lockfile is the contract'
cargo build -q --locked 2>&1 && echo '[--locked build ok]'
sed -i 's/^url = "2.5"/url = "=2.5.4"/' Cargo.toml
cargo build -q --locked 2>&1 | head -3
echo "[--locked build exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}]"
--- claim a newer MSRV than this toolchain
error: rustc 1.85.1 is not supported by the following package:
  msrv-lab@0.1.0 requires rustc 1.90

[cargo build exit 101]
--- the escape hatch (use when you know why)
[build ok with --ignore-rust-version]
--- CI: the lockfile is the contract
[--locked build ok]
error: the lock file /tmp/msrv-lab/Cargo.lock needs to be updated but --locked was passed to prevent this
If you want to try to generate the lock file without accessing the network, remove the --locked flag and use --offline instead.
[--locked build exit 101]

Claiming rust-version = "1.90" makes Cargo reject your own package on 1.85.1 with a clear message, before rustc can fail on some syntax error deep in your code. That is what the field is for.
--ignore-rust-version builds anyway. Use it when you know the newer feature is behind a cfg you do not hit, not as a habit.
--locked makes the committed lockfile the contract. When the manifest and the lockfile disagree, CI fails instead of silently resolving a new graph. That is how you stop a CI run from picking up a transitive update that nobody reviewed.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
section: Case 5 — No rust-version? Then your toolchain is the MSRV
text:
Case 5 — No rust-version? Then your toolchain is the MSRV
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-05-no-msrv.sh — no rust-version at all: what does resolver "3" compare against?
set -uo pipefail
cd /tmp/msrv-lab
sed -i 's/^url = "=2.5.4"/url = "2.5"/; /^rust-version = /d' Cargo.toml
grep -E '^(edition|rust-version|resolver)' Cargo.toml
rm -f Cargo.lock
cargo generate-lockfile 2>&1 | grep -E 'Locking|uuid|icu_normalizer '
cargo build -q 2>&1 && echo '[build ok on rustc 1.85.1]'
edition = "2021"          # resolver "2": rust-version of deps is ignored
resolver = "3"             # default for edition 2024; needs Cargo 1.84+
     Locking 53 packages to latest Rust 1.85.1 compatible versions
      Adding icu_normalizer v2.1.1 (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding uuid v1.26.1 (available: v1.28.0, requires Rust 1.89.0)
[build ok on rustc 1.85.1]
With rust-version removed, resolver "3" resolved against “Rust 1.85.1”, the toolchain running cargo. That is convenient on one machine and a trap on a team. A developer on 1.99 and a CI runner on 1.85 generate different lockfiles from the same manifest. Declare rust-version and the result no longer depends on who ran cargo update.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
section: Case 6 — Check the MSRV in CI (configuration, not run here)
text:
Case 6 — Check the MSRV in CI (configuration, not run here)
This needs a second toolchain (rustup toolchain install), which this box does not have, so it was not run. It is the pattern the Cargo book’s “Rust version” chapter and its CI guide describe: verify the MSRV with the lockfile you ship.
# .github/workflows/msrv.yml — build the committed Cargo.lock on the declared MSRV
name: msrv
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  msrv:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: rustup toolchain install 1.85 --profile minimal
      - run: cargo +1.85 check --locked --all-targets
Pair it with a normal job on the latest stable, so you also see breakage that a newer compiler would catch. For libraries, remember that downstream users do not use your Cargo.lock. Their resolver, their rust-version and their toolchain decide what they get. The rust-version field on every crate in the graph is what lets their resolver choose well.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
The trap
The trap is reading MSRV as “the oldest compiler that compiles my code”. You test once on the old toolchain, it works, and you ship. Weeks later a routine cargo update, or a fresh clone without a lockfile, pulls icu_normalizer 2.3.0 three levels down, and the MSRV build fails with no change to your code. The two usual fixes make it worse. Pinning the transitive crate with = in your own Cargo.toml freezes it for every downstream user. Dropping rust-version makes Cargo resolve against whichever toolchain happens to run, so the lockfile changes from one machine to the next.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
The boring rule

Declare package.rust-version. Use resolver "3" (edition 2024 gives it to you). Let cargo add choose versions. Commit Cargo.lock for applications and build with --locked in CI. Keep one CI job on the declared MSRV and one on latest stable. When a dependency needs a newer compiler, decide deliberately: raise rust-version (a minor-version bump per the Cargo book) or keep the older dependency. Don’t hand-pin transitive crates.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
Try this

In /tmp/msrv-lab, set resolver = "2", run cargo update, and confirm the ICU crates jump back to 2.3.0. Then set CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_RUST_VERSIONS=fallback for one cargo update and compare.
Raise rust-version to "1.88", run cargo update, and read which Downgrading notes turn into Updating.
Use cargo update icu_normalizer@2.1.1 --precise 2.3.0 with resolver "3". What does --precise do to the MSRV policy?
Add a second workspace member with no rust-version that also depends on url = "2.5". Which idna_adapter does the shared lockfile get, and why? (Hint: version unification in the resolver chapter.)
On a machine with rustup, run the Case 6 workflow steps locally (cargo +1.85 check --locked --all-targets) against one of your own crates.

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text:
Thesis
Adding a dependency doesn’t just add code to your binary. It adds code that runs on your machine at build time. The Cargo reference puts it plainly: placing a file named build.rs in a package root “will cause Cargo to compile that script and execute it just before building the package” (Build Scripts). Procedural macros are the same: they are compiler plugins that run inside rustc. Neither is sandboxed. They run with your user, your environment, your files and your network.
That is why typosquatting works so well against Rust developers: a crate named almost like proc-macro2 only has to be built to act. This chapter shows exactly when that code runs, using a harmless look-alike crate, and what a simple sandbox does and doesn’t stop.



When does dependency code run on your machine?

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text:
When it runs
#!/bin/sh
cd "$(dirname "$0")/app"
set -x
cargo metadata --format-version 1 --offline > /dev/null; ls /tmp/buildrs-was-here
cargo check --offline 2>&1 | grep -v "^ *Finished\|^ *Checking\|^ *Compiling"
cat /tmp/buildrs-was-here
rm -f /tmp/buildrs-was-here; cargo clean -q
unshare -rn cargo check --offline 2>&1 | grep -v "^ *Finished\|^ *Checking\|^ *Compiling"
cat /tmp/buildrs-was-here
Output with cargo 1.99.1 on Linux:
+ cargo metadata --format-version 1 --offline
+ ls /tmp/buildrs-was-here
ls: cannot access '/tmp/buildrs-was-here': No such file or directory
+ cargo check --offline
+ grep -v ^ *Finished\|^ *Checking\|^ *Compiling
warning: proc-macro-two@0.1.0: build.rs ran as uid 1000: saw 111 env vars, 0 entries in ~/.ssh; network: connected to 1.1.1.1:443
+ cat /tmp/buildrs-was-here
build.rs ran as uid 1000: saw 111 env vars, 0 entries in ~/.ssh; network: connected to 1.1.1.1:443
+ rm -f /tmp/buildrs-was-here
+ cargo clean -q
+ unshare -rn cargo check --offline
+ grep -v ^ *Finished\|^ *Checking\|^ *Compiling
warning: proc-macro-two@0.1.0: build.rs ran as uid 0: saw 111 env vars, 0 entries in ~/.ssh; network: Network is unreachable (os error 101)
+ cat /tmp/buildrs-was-here
build.rs ran as uid 0: saw 111 env vars, 0 entries in ~/.ssh; network: Network is unreachable (os error 101)
What happened:

cargo metadata didn’t run it. Resolving the dependency graph is safe, so the marker file doesn’t exist yet.
cargo check ran it, even though check produces no binary. The build script ran as uid 1000 (the developer), saw all 111 environment variables, reached 1.1.1.1:443 on the internet, and wrote /tmp/buildrs-was-here. A real attack would have sent the variables instead of counting them.
Editors do the same. rust-analyzer’s rust-analyzer.cargo.buildScripts.enable defaults to true (“Run build scripts (build.rs) for more precise code analysis”), and proc-macro support implies it (configuration). Opening a cloned repository in your editor can be enough.
A namespace sandbox is partial. Under unshare -rn (a new user namespace mapping you to uid 0, plus an empty network namespace), the connection fails with Network is unreachable. The script still read the environment and still wrote to /tmp on the host. To contain the filesystem too, you need a container or VM with only the source tree mounted, or a dedicated build user.

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text:
Defences, in order of payoff

Watch what enters Cargo.lock. Most attacks need a new package name: a typo, a look-alike, or a dependency confusion. Review lockfile diffs in PRs like code, and build in CI with cargo build --locked so nothing is resolved silently.
Audit before you trust. cargo-vet records which crate versions “have been audited by a trusted entity” and fails CI for unaudited ones. cargo-deny can ban crates, restrict sources to crates.io or known git hosts, and check RustSec advisories.
Vendor for hermetic builds. cargo vendor plus --offline makes the build use exactly the reviewed sources.
Sandbox untrusted builds, including the first build of a cloned repository and any editor session in one. Cut both the network and the host filesystem, as the namespace experiment above shows.
Keep secrets out of build environments. A build job that doesn’t need a publish token shouldn’t have one. Everything in env::vars() is readable by every build script in the graph.

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text:
Takeaways

build.rs and proc macros run at build time, as you, with full access. cargo check and your editor trigger them, while cargo metadata doesn’t.
A look-alike name is the whole attack. Lockfile review, --locked, and cargo-vet or cargo-deny stop it before it builds.
Sandboxes have to cover the network and the filesystem: unshare -rn alone left the host file write intact.

title: Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
text:
Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
After reading this chapter, you will understand how Cargo’s dependency publish-age cooldown policy protects your project against supply-chain compromise, how to configure global and per-registry cooldown thresholds in config.toml, and how Cargo’s resolver responds when candidate crate versions are too young.
Supply-chain attacks on package registries frequently rely on speed. When an attacker compromises a popular crate maintainer’s credentials or takes over an abandoned package, they publish a malicious version and rely on automated CI runs or cargo update calls to pull it into downstream projects before human auditors or automated scanners detect the breach.
Stabilized in Rust 1.100, Cargo’s min-publish-age resolver feature creates an automatic safety buffer (or “cooldown period”) for newly published crate versions. By configuring Cargo to ignore releases published within a specific window—such as 7 days—your builds automatically reject fresh releases until the community has had time to inspect and report potential security issues.

title: Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
text:
Supply-Chain Window of Vulnerability
When a new package version is uploaded to crates.io, it is immediately available for download by cargo clients. Security advisories, maintainer revokations, and automated security scanning tools take time to catch compromised releases.
Timeline of a Package Compromise:
T+00h: Attacker publishes malicious version 1.2.4
T+01h: CI pipelines running `cargo update` pull version 1.2.4  <-- Vulnerability Window
T+12h: Security researcher discovers payload and files advisory
T+14h: Crates.io maintainers yank version 1.2.4
Without a publish-age policy, any build resolving unpinned dependencies during the vulnerability window pulls version 1.2.4. With a min-publish-age policy of 7 days, Cargo’s resolver acts as if version 1.2.4 does not exist during those first seven days, falling back to the latest version that satisfies both your semver requirement and the age criteria (such as version 1.2.3).

title: Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
text:
Configuring min-publish-age
Cargo supports configuring minimum publish-age rules across all registries or on a per-registry basis inside your Cargo configuration file (.cargo/config.toml or ~/.cargo/config.toml).
# config.toml
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "7 days"

[resolver]
incompatible-publish-age = "deny"

Configuration Parameters









Key
Section
Accepted Values
Description




global-min-publish-age
[registry]
Human-readable duration (e.g., "7 days", "48 hours")
Sets the default minimum age required for all candidate versions across all registries.


min-publish-age
[registries.<name>]
Human-readable duration
Overrides global-min-publish-age for a specific named registry.


incompatible-publish-age
[resolver]
"deny", "allow", "warn"
Controls Cargo’s resolver behavior when a candidate crate version fails the publish-age check.



For internal private registries where packages are built and verified within your own infrastructure, you can override the global default to zero:
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "7 days"

[registries.internal-corp]
index = "https://crates.internal.example.com/index"
min-publish-age = "0 days"

title: Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
text:
Resolver Policy Modes
The resolver.incompatible-publish-age configuration option defines how strictly Cargo enforces publish age when resolving your dependency graph:

deny (Default / Recommended): Cargo rejects any candidate version published more recently than the minimum publish age. If a Cargo.toml explicitly requests a version that violates this policy, Cargo halts with a resolution error.
allow: Cargo ignores the publish-age policy completely, permitting any published version regardless of age.
warn: Cargo resolves the newest semver-compatible version (even if younger than the minimum publish age), but emits a warning log informing the developer that a newly published version was selected.







Note



Not run here. The local environment in this demonstration runs rustc/cargo 1.99.1. The min-publish-age and incompatible-publish-age options require Rust 1.100 or newer. On versions prior to Rust 1.100, these configuration options are unvalidated or ignored by Cargo.

title: Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
section: How min-publish-age Fits into Rust Security Defenses
text:
How min-publish-age Fits into Rust Security Defenses
min-publish-age addresses a specific risk window in the Rust ecosystem. It works alongside existing supply-chain tools:

Cargo.lock & cargo build --locked: Pins exact versions across builds. min-publish-age takes effect when running cargo update or when adding new dependencies, preventing initial inclusion of premature releases.
cargo-vet: Manages peer-reviewed audits of dependency source code. cargo-vet requires explicit human approval for code changes, whereas min-publish-age provides an automated time-based safeguard for un-audited minor/patch updates.
cargo-audit & cargo-deny: Scans Cargo.lock against known vulnerability databases (RustSec). These tools depend on advisories being filed after a flaw is discovered; min-publish-age protects builds during the time gap before an advisory is published.









Tool / Mechanism
Defense Trigger
Primary Protection




Cargo.lock
Build time (--locked)
Deterministic builds, prevents drift


min-publish-age
Resolution time (cargo update)
Supply-chain cooldown buffer against fresh publishes


cargo-vet
Audit verification
Code review and trust verification


cargo-audit
Vulnerability scanning
Known CVE / RustSec advisory matching

title: Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
text:
Pitfalls

Broken emergency hotfixes: If an upstream crate releases a critical bugfix or security patch, your build will reject it until the package reaches the min-publish-age threshold. For emergency updates, temporarily lower the duration in .cargo/config.toml or override the resolver behavior via CLI flags.
Private registries blocking builds: CI pipelines relying on private, internal registries will fail if internal packages are deployed and consumed within the cooldown window. Always configure registries.<name>.min-publish-age = "0 days" for internal registries.
Offline builds: min-publish-age relies on index metadata timestamps. In offline mode (--offline), Cargo relies on cached registry index timestamp metadata.

title: Cargo min-publish-age: dependency cooldowns against fresh crates.io publishes
text:
Key takeaways

min-publish-age is a Cargo resolver policy stabilized in Rust 1.100 that skips crate versions younger than a configured duration.
Configured in .cargo/config.toml under [registry] (global-min-publish-age) and [resolver] (incompatible-publish-age).
Protects projects during the initial window of vulnerability before malicious publishes are discovered and yanked from crates.io.
Complements exact version locking (Cargo.lock), code auditing (cargo-vet), and advisory scanners (cargo-audit).

title: Servo 0.1: Embeddable Engine on crates.io
text: Servo 0.1: Embeddable Engine on crates.io

title: Servo 0.1: Embeddable Engine on crates.io
text:
Thesis
On 2026-04-13 the Servo project published servo 0.1.0 on crates.io — the first release of the engine as a library, not only as the servoshell demo browser. The 0.1 version number is deliberate: the team has not defined what 1.0 means yet, but the bump signals growing confidence that the embedding API is usable for real embedders. Monthly crates keep moving (by late 2026 the crate line includes 0.7.x regular releases plus a parallel 0.1.x LTS line). This chapter teaches the mental model of embedding Servo: what the crate is for, what 0.1 vs LTS vs monthly means, and which build/feature knobs matter — without downloading the engine’s enormous dependency graph in the book lab.
Toolchain note: examples assume a recent stable Rust. This authoring host has rustc 1.99.0. Current servo releases advertise MSRV 1.88.0 (see crates.io); LTS migration notes may raise clang and Rust floors when you jump major LTS lines.

title: Servo 0.1: Embeddable Engine on crates.io
text:
Mental model
  Your application (windowing, input, IPC, privileges)
           │
           │  embedding API (servo crate + embedder traits)
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Servo library                                        │
  │  constellation · script · layout · paint · net · …    │
  │  optional: webgl / webgpu / webxr / media-gstreamer   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
           │
           ▼
  OS graphics / audio / network backends (surfman, etc.)







Concept
Meaning




servo crate
The embeddable engine on crates.io (MPL-2.0)


servoshell
Demo browser — not published to crates.io; build from the GitHub tree


0.1.0 milestone
First library release; embedding API “good enough for some users,” not a stability covenant


Monthly / regular line
Fast-moving; breaking changes expected between minors


LTS line
Best-effort ~6-month cadence, ~9-month support, security fixes only; may need git deps for CVE backports


servo-embedder-traits
Hooks embedders implement (e.g. custom resource readers)


baked-in-resources / bundled
Default path that embeds default resources in the binary; disable and supply your own reader if you need that



Risk profile (from the Servo book): rendering known, trusted content inside your app is a different threat model from a general-purpose browser that loads the open web. Evaluate accordingly — Servo is still pre-1.0.

title: Servo 0.1: Embeddable Engine on crates.io
Servo 0.1: Embeddable Engine on crates.io
text:
The trap

Publishing or depending on servoshell. The demo browser is not the embeddable product line on crates.io.
Assuming crates.io LTS patches always exist. Security backports may force git dependencies when MSRV blocks a crates.io bump — plan for that in corporate allow-lists.
Leaving default features on “for convenience” on constrained devices. Media, WebGL, WebGPU, and WebXR are heavy; turn on what you need.
Treating 0.1 as production-complete. The project is explicit: no 1.0 definition yet. Trusted-content widgets ≠ full browser replacement.
Skipping resource ownership. If you disable baked-in resources and forget a ResourceReader, startup fails in confusing ways. The OpenHarmony example is the reference pattern.

title: Servo 0.1: Embeddable Engine on crates.io
text:
The boring rule
Depend on the servo library crate, pick regular vs LTS on purpose, keep servoshell out of your Cargo.toml, and follow book.servo.org/embedding for the builder/event-loop API on the version you pinned. Evaluate threat model before you point the engine at untrusted URLs.

title: The Rust Compilation Pipeline
text:
The Rust Compilation Pipeline
Understanding how rustc compiles code: 1. Parsing & Macro Expansion -> AST 2. HIR (High-level Intermediate Representation) -> Type checking 3. MIR (Mid-level Intermediate Representation) -> Borrow checker & optimizations 4. LLVM IR -> Native machine code generation

title: A Tiny JIT with Cranelift: From Postfix Expressions to Native Code
text:
A Tiny JIT with Cranelift: From Postfix Expressions to Native Code
After reading this chapter, you will be able to parse a reverse Polish notation (RPN) arithmetic expression, lower it into Cranelift Intermediate Representation (IR) using single static assignment (SSA) values, compile that IR in-process into executable machine code, and invoke the resulting function safely through a Rust function pointer.

title: A Tiny JIT with Cranelift: From Postfix Expressions to Native Code
text:
Thesis
A JIT doesn’t have to mean writing machine code by hand or linking LLVM. Cranelift is a code generator written in Rust. It is the compiler inside Wasmtime and the backend of rustc_codegen_cranelift, which can stand in for LLVM to give faster debug builds. You build SSA-form IR through its API and it emits native code for the host, in-process, at runtime.
In this chapter, a postfix expression typed at runtime becomes a native function you call through a function pointer, in about 150 lines. We check its results against a plain interpreter and time both. Only two lines are unsafe, and the chapter explains what each one depends on.

title: A Tiny JIT with Cranelift: From Postfix Expressions to Native Code
text:
When a JIT pays off
A JIT is a trade. You pay to compile up front, ship a code generator in your binary and take on unsafe code. In return each later evaluation is cheap.
JIT compilation pays off when an expression or program is evaluated repeatedly over a large dataset or long runtime:

Hot user-supplied expressions: Database filter predicates, dynamic routing rules, spreadsheet formulas, or financial risk calculations compiled once and run against many records.
Emulators and language runtimes: Dynamic translation of foreign ISA instructions or language bytecode into host native code.
Small DSLs and rules engines where an interpreter is the bottleneck.

Conversely, avoid JIT compilation under the following conditions:

One-off execution: If an expression is evaluated only a handful of times, building IR and emitting code costs more than just interpreting it.
Platform restrictions: Environments enforcing strict W^X (Write XOR Execute) memory policies without permissions for executable heap allocation (such as iOS or locked-down sandbox environments) prohibit in-process JIT compilation.
Security-sensitive boundaries: Native memory execution increases the attack surface if untrusted inputs can influence codegen in ways that bypass bounds checks or memory isolation.

title: A Tiny JIT with Cranelift: From Postfix Expressions to Native Code

The Cranelift crate ecosystem
Cranelift is modularized into several focused crates. The JIT pipeline relies on five primary crates, all at version 0.137.1:








Crate
Primary Purpose

FunctionBuilder, FunctionBuilderContext

Module, Linkage


cranelift-jit

JITModule, JITBuilder
